title: Stoichiometry: counting atoms by weighing
summary: Students learn the mole, molar mass, balanced equations, mole ratios, limiting reactants and percent yield. Two labs and a unit test check the skills.
brief: Stoichiometry for grade 10 chemistry: ten 55-minute lessons on the mole, molar mass, balancing equations, mole ratios, limiting reactants and percent yield. Two labs: a baking soda and vinegar reaction to find the mass of carbon dioxide released, and a copper chloride and aluminum foil reaction to find the limiting reactant, each with a lab report. Problem sets twice a week. Grading: lab reports 30%, problem sets 20%, unit test 50%.
policies:
Goggles, apron and closed-toe shoes are required on lab days; a student without them observes and writes up the data from a partner. No food or drink in the lab.

Problem sets are due at the start of the next class after they are set. Late sets lose 10% a day, up to three days.

Lab reports are written individually from data collected with a partner; shared data is fine, shared wording is not.

Bring a scientific calculator and a periodic table every day. The unit test allows both.

l_591e0e38090f.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
l_591e0e38090f.summary: Students learn why chemists count particles in moles and use Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³, to convert between moles and particles.

segments.title: Counting a bag of rice without counting
segments.description:
Show a sealed bag of rice and a balance. Count out 20 grains as a class and find their mass.
Then weigh the whole bag. Remove the rice, weigh the empty bag, and subtract its mass from the full bag’s mass. Pairs estimate how many grains the bag holds without counting them, and share their method.
Ask: how could we do the same for atoms?
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare ahead: bag of rice, balance, a spare set of 20 grains counted in advance, in case the class count runs long. Example: 20 grains = 0.50 g, bag = 250 g, so 250 ÷ 0.025 = 10,000 grains. Students often try to count; steer them to mass per grain. Safety: rice is not for eating; sweep up spilled grains, which are a slip hazard.

segments.title: Why chemists count in moles
segments.description:
Compare counting words: a pair is 2, a dozen is 12, a ream of paper is 500 sheets.
Introduce the mole as a counting word for 6.022 × 10²³ particles, called Avogadro’s number.
Show that counting one particle per second would take about 1.9 × 10¹⁶ years, while the universe is about 1.38 × 10¹⁰ years old.
Name the particle types: atoms of Na, molecules of H₂O, formula units of NaCl.
segments.teacherNotes: Check: 6.022 × 10²³ s ÷ 3.156 × 10⁷ s per year ≈ 1.9 × 10¹⁶ years. Misconception: a mole is a mass. It is a number, like a dozen. Write the number in scientific notation and read it aloud as ‘six point zero two two times ten to the twenty-third’.

segments.title: Converting between moles and particles
segments.description:
Model the conversion factor 6.022 × 10²³ particles / 1 mol, with units written at every step.
Work 2.50 mol of H₂O molecules, multiplying to find the number of molecules.
Then work 3.01 × 10²³ atoms of Al, dividing to find the moles.
Students say aloud which operation is needed and why before each calculation.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 2.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.5055 × 10²⁴, so 1.51 × 10²⁴ molecules. 3.01 × 10²³ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 0.500 mol. Common mistake: multiplying when they should divide. Tip: put mol in the conversion factor’s denominator when starting with moles, and put particles in its denominator when starting with particles. Cancel matching units to check the setup. Keep three significant figures.

segments.title: Mole and particle conversions
segments.description:
Students work five conversions in pairs, showing the unit setup for each.
After every two problems, pairs swap papers with a neighboring pair and compare answers.
The teacher circulates and checks that exponents are handled correctly on the calculator.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. 2.00 mol CO₂ molecules to molecules: 1.20 × 10²⁴
2. 0.250 mol Na atoms to atoms: 1.51 × 10²³
3. 1.20 × 10²⁴ Mg atoms to moles: 1.99 mol
4. 9.03 × 10²³ H₂O molecules to moles: 1.50 mol
5. 3.50 mol H₂O: total atoms? 3.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.11 × 10²⁴ molecules; × 3 atoms per molecule = 6.32 × 10²⁴ atoms
Mistake: entering ×10²³ as ×10×23 on the calculator; show the EE key.

segments.title: Same moles, different stuff
segments.description:
Ask: if we have 1 mol of water molecules and 1 mol of sodium atoms, do we have the same number of particles?
Ask: would the two samples have the same mass? Why might they differ?
Collect ideas from a few pairs without confirming the mass answer yet.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: same number of particles, 6.022 × 10²³ each, but different mass because the particles differ. This prepares for molar mass later in the course. Accept guesses; do not teach molar mass here. Common mistake: thinking a mole of a heavier atom has more particles.

segments.title: Two-question exit check
segments.description:
Students answer two questions on a half sheet, working alone and without notes.
The class then checks answers together by a show of hands on the final values.
segments.teacherNotes:
Not graded. Q1: A sample holds 0.400 mol of copper atoms. How many copper atoms is that? Show your setup. Answer: 0.400 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.41 × 10²³ atoms.
Q2: A flask holds 1.81 × 10²⁴ molecules of O₂. How many moles is that? Answer: 1.81 × 10²⁴ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.01 mol.

segments.title: Summing up the mole
segments.description:
Students finish this sentence aloud in unison: one mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, so to find particles I multiply, and to find moles I divide.
Collect the half sheets as students leave.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the half sheets to spot who still multiplies and divides the wrong way, and plan a quick review for those students.

keyIdeas: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count one at a time, so chemists count them in groups, the way we count eggs by the dozen.
One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles. This value is called Avogadro’s number.
The particles can be atoms, molecules or formula units. The word mole names an amount, not a kind of particle.
To convert moles to particles, multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole. To convert particles to moles, divide by the same number.
Check every answer: a number of moles is usually small, and a number of particles is huge.

study.overview: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count one at a time, so chemists count them in groups called moles. One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, a number called Avogadro’s number. This guide shows what a mole is, how to convert between moles and particles, and how to check that your answer makes sense.

points.heading: The mole is a counting word, like a dozen
points.explanation: We use words for groups: a pair is 2, a dozen is 12, a ream of paper is 500 sheets. A mole is a counting word for 6.022 × 10²³ particles. It is a number, not a mass. Chemists need it because atoms are too small to count one by one. Even counting one particle per second would take about 1.9 × 10¹⁶ years, and the universe is only about 1.38 × 10¹⁰ years old. The same idea worked with the bag of rice: you find the mass of a small counted group, then use it to work out the count of the whole bag without counting every grain. Example: 20 grains had a mass of 0.50 g, and the rice in the bag had a mass of 250 g, so the bag held 250 ÷ 0.025 = 10,000 grains.

points.heading: Particles can be atoms, molecules or formula units
points.explanation: The word mole names an amount, not a kind of particle. The particles can be atoms, molecules or formula units. Examples: 1 mol of Na is 6.022 × 10²³ atoms of Na. 1 mol of H₂O is 6.022 × 10²³ molecules of H₂O. 1 mol of NaCl is 6.022 × 10²³ formula units of NaCl. So 1 mol of water molecules and 1 mol of sodium atoms hold the same number of particles. A mole of a heavier atom does not have more particles. Whether the two samples have the same mass is a question we will return to later in the course.

points.heading: Converting between moles and particles
points.explanation: Use the conversion factor 6.022 × 10²³ particles / 1 mol, and write the units at every step. To go from moles to particles, multiply, with mol in the denominator so it cancels. To go from particles to moles, divide, with particles in the denominator. Example 1: 2.50 mol of H₂O molecules × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 1.5055 × 10²⁴, so 1.51 × 10²⁴ molecules. Example 2: 3.01 × 10²³ atoms of Al ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol = 0.500 mol. Before you calculate, say which operation you need and why. A common mistake is to multiply when you should divide. On a calculator, enter ×10²³ with the EE key, not as ×10×23. Keep three significant figures.

points.heading: Check that your answer makes sense
points.explanation: A number of moles is usually small, like 0.500 or 3.01. A number of particles is huge, with an exponent such as 10²³ or 10²⁴. If you convert moles to particles and get a small number, you divided when you should have multiplied. If you convert particles to moles and get a huge number, you multiplied when you should have divided. Also cancel the units: if they do not leave the unit you want, the setup is wrong. Remember: one mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, so to find particles I multiply, and to find moles I divide.

l_ec61138c9f4d.summary: Students find molar mass from the periodic table for elements and compounds such as H₂O and NaHCO₃.

segments.title: Same moles, different mass
segments.description:
Return the exit half sheets and put last time’s question back on the board: 1 mol of water molecules and 1 mol of sodium atoms hold the same number of particles, but do they have the same mass?
Pairs write one reason for their guess.
Reveal the two masses: 1 mol of sodium atoms is 22.99 g and 1 mol of water molecules is 18.02 g. Ask what differs between the two kinds of particle.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: same number of particles, 6.022 × 10²³ each, but different mass because the particles differ. Use the half sheets to seat students who still mixed up multiplying and dividing beside a confident partner. Do not use sodium metal in class; show the value on the board.

segments.title: Molar mass of an element
segments.description:
Define molar mass as the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol.
On a periodic table, point to the atomic mass under each symbol. Read it two ways: the mass of one atom in atomic mass units, and the mass of one mole of atoms in grams.
Work three elements aloud: carbon 12.01 g/mol, copper 63.55 g/mol, aluminum 26.98 g/mol.
Students write each value with its unit.
segments.teacherNotes: Round atomic masses to two decimal places and use the same table all unit. Common mistake: writing the number without g/mol. Say the unit aloud every time. Remind students that a mole is a number, not a mass, so molar mass is the mass of that many particles.

segments.title: Seeing one mole on the balance
segments.description:
Show three labeled containers, each holding one mole: water, table salt (NaCl) and aluminum foil.
Weigh each on the balance and write the readings: 18.02 g, 58.44 g and 26.98 g.
Ask: each container holds 6.022 × 10²³ particles, so what does molar mass connect?
Take answers from a few pairs and record the class’s sentence on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare ahead: 18.02 g of water in a beaker, 58.44 g of NaCl in a labeled sealed cup, and 26.98 g of foil, torn to size. Tare each empty container, including the cup’s lid, before adding its sample. When weighing the prepared samples in class, subtract the recorded container masses to display the sample masses. Safety: nothing from the demonstration is tasted or taken out of the room. Wipe up spills at once. Expected idea: molar mass links mass to number of particles.

segments.title: Molar mass of a compound
segments.description:
Model H₂O in a table: element, atoms in the formula, molar mass, and subtotal. H gives 2 × 1.01 = 2.02 and O gives 1 × 16.00 = 16.00. The total is 18.02 g/mol.
Now work NaHCO₃ the same way, with students calling out each subscript.
The total is 84.01 g/mol. Link it to baking soda, which students will use in a lab later in the course.
segments.teacherNotes: NaHCO₃: Na 22.99 + H 1.01 + C 12.01 + O 3 × 16.00 = 48.00, total 84.01 g/mol. Common mistakes: counting O once in NaHCO₃, and forgetting the unit. Insist on the table layout. Students may not yet know how a subscript applies after parentheses; introduce that in the practice.

segments.title: Five molar masses in pairs
segments.description:
Before pairs begin, explain that a subscript outside parentheses multiplies every atom count inside. Model Ca(OH)₂: one Ca atom, two O atoms and two H atoms. Pairs then work five molar masses, writing the table for every compound.
After the second and fourth problems, pairs compare totals with a neighboring pair and settle any difference by recounting atoms.
The teacher circulates and checks subscripts, parentheses and units.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Cu: 63.55 g/mol
2. CO₂: 12.01 + 2 × 16.00 = 44.01 g/mol
3. NaCl: 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 g/mol
4. Al(OH)₃: 26.98 + 3 × (16.00 + 1.01) = 78.01 g/mol
5. C₂H₄O₂ (acetic acid, in vinegar): 24.02 + 4.04 + 32.00 = 60.06 g/mol
Twelve minutes is tight once Ca(OH)₂ has been modelled. If pairs fall behind, skip item 1, which only repeats a table lookup, and keep items 4 and 5.
Mistake: ignoring the subscript outside the parentheses.

segments.title: Two-question exit check
segments.description:
Students answer two questions on a half sheet, alone and without notes.
Then the class checks the final values together by a show of hands.
segments.teacherNotes: Not graded. Q1: Find the molar mass of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂. Show your table. Answer: 24.31 + 2 × (16.00 + 1.01) = 58.33 g/mol. Q2: In one sentence, say what molar mass links together. Answer: the mass of a sample in grams and the number of particles in it, through the mole. Collect sheets to plan review.

segments.title: Summing up molar mass
segments.description:
Students finish the sentence aloud in unison: molar mass is the mass of one mole, found by adding the atomic masses in the formula, and it links grams to particles.
Preview next time: students will use molar mass to turn grams into moles.
Collect the half sheets as students leave.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the sheets to spot students who leave out g/mol or miscount subscripts. Plan a short review for them before conversions begin. No homework is set.

keyIdeas: Molar mass is the mass in grams of one mole of a substance. Its unit is grams per mole (g/mol).
For an element, the molar mass is the atomic mass on the periodic table, read in g/mol. Carbon’s atomic mass of 12.01 gives 12.01 g/mol.
For a compound, add the molar masses of every atom in the formula. A subscript tells you how many times to count that atom.
Molar mass links the mass of a sample, which we can weigh, to the number of particles in it, which we cannot count. One mole of any substance holds 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

points.heading: Molar mass of an element
points.explanation: For an element, the molar mass is the atomic mass on the periodic table, read in g/mol. The same number has two readings. It is the mass of one atom in atomic mass units, and the mass of one mole of atoms in grams. Always write the unit. Example: carbon has an atomic mass of 12.01, so its molar mass is 12.01 g/mol. Copper is 63.55 g/mol and aluminum is 26.98 g/mol. Use the same periodic table each time and round to two decimal places.

points.heading: Molar mass of a compound
points.explanation: For a compound, add the molar masses of every atom in the formula. A subscript tells you how many times to count that atom. A table helps: list the element, the number of atoms, the molar mass, and the subtotal. Example: H₂O has 2 H atoms and 1 O atom. H gives 2 × 1.01 = 2.02. O gives 1 × 16.00 = 16.00. The total is 18.02 g/mol. For NaHCO₃: Na 22.99 + H 1.01 + C 12.01 + O 3 × 16.00 = 48.00, so the total is 84.01 g/mol. A common mistake is counting O only once. Another is leaving out g/mol.

points.heading: Subscripts outside parentheses
points.explanation: A subscript outside parentheses multiplies every atom count inside them. Example: Ca(OH)₂ has 1 Ca atom, 2 O atoms and 2 H atoms. The molar mass is 40.08 + 2 × (16.00 + 1.01) = 74.10 g/mol. Do not ignore the 2 outside the parentheses. If you and a partner get different totals, recount the atoms one element at a time.

points.heading: What molar mass links together
points.explanation: Molar mass connects grams to particles through the mole. In class, one mole of water (18.02 g), table salt NaCl (58.44 g) and aluminum foil (26.98 g) each held 6.022 × 10²³ particles, yet the masses were different. So you can weigh a sample and know how many particles it holds. Next time you will use molar mass to turn grams into moles. Remember the sentence from class: molar mass is the mass of one mole, found by adding the atomic masses in the formula, and it links grams to particles.

segments.title: Molar mass check and return of half sheets
segments.description:
Return last time’s exit half sheets and write on the board: find the molar mass of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃.
Students build the element table alone, then compare totals with a partner.
Take the total from one pair and have the class say aloud the unit it carries.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2 × 22.99 + 12.01 + 3 × 16.00 = 105.99 g/mol. Common mistakes: counting Na once, omitting g/mol. Use the half sheets to pair students who still miscount subscripts with a confident partner.

segments.title: Converting between grams and moles
segments.description:
Show last time’s sealed cup of NaCl, which holds one mole at 58.44 g. Ask how many moles half the original mass of salt would contain, then work 29.22 g NaCl as a setup: 29.22 g × (1 mol / 58.44 g) = 0.500 mol.
Point out that grams cancel and moles remain.
Work the reverse with 2.00 mol H₂O: 2.00 mol × (18.02 g / 1 mol) = 36.0 g.
Students say aloud which unit goes on the bottom of the factor before each setup.
segments.teacherNotes: Model putting the unit you want to cancel in the denominator. Common mistake: dividing when they should multiply. Introduce dimensional analysis and significant figures here; use three significant figures for final answers. Keep the unrounded calculator value between steps; any rounded intermediate value shown is for display only. Safety: sealed NaCl is not for eating, wipe up spills, and weigh only prepared samples.

segments.title: Grams and moles in pairs
segments.description:
Pairs work three conversions between grams and moles, writing the unit setup for each.
After the second problem, pairs swap papers with a neighboring pair and compare answers.
The teacher circulates and checks that molar masses are found first and units cancel.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. 25.0 g CO₂ to moles: 25.0 ÷ 44.01 = 0.568 mol
2. 0.250 mol Cu to grams: 0.250 × 63.55 = 15.9 g
3. 4.00 g NaHCO₃ to moles: 4.00 ÷ 84.01 = 0.0476 mol
Watch for forgotten molar mass lookups.

segments.title: Mass to particles in two steps
segments.description:
Pose the question: how many atoms are in a 10.0 g piece of aluminum foil?
Draw two arrows on the board: grams to moles using 26.98 g/mol, then moles to atoms using the factor from earlier in the course.
Work it as one chain: 10.0 g × (1 mol / 26.98 g) × (6.022 × 10²³ atoms / 1 mol), and have students enter it on the calculator step by step.
Ask students to judge whether the size of the answer makes sense.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 10.0 ÷ 26.98 = 0.371 mol; × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.23 × 10²³ atoms. Common mistake: skipping the mole step or retyping exponents wrongly. Safety: foil edges can cut; handle carefully.

segments.title: Two-step problems
segments.description:
Pairs work two problems, one going from mass to particles and one going from particles to mass.
Students write the full unit chain before touching the calculator.
Pairs that finish early explain to each other where moles appear in the middle of each chain.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
4. 9.00 g H₂O to molecules: 9.00 ÷ 18.02 = 0.499 mol; × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules
5. 1.20 × 10²⁴ Mg atoms to grams: ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.99 mol; × 24.31 = 48.4 g

segments.title: Two-question exit check
segments.description:
Students answer two questions on a half sheet, working alone and without notes.
The class then checks the final values together by a show of hands.
segments.teacherNotes:
Not graded.
Q1: How many moles are in 20.0 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH? Show your setup. Answer: 20.0 ÷ 40.00 = 0.500 mol.
Q2: How many copper atoms are in 6.35 g of copper? Show both steps. Answer: 6.35 ÷ 63.55 = 0.0999 mol; × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² atoms.

segments.title: Summing up and homework
segments.description:
Students finish the sentence aloud in unison: to go between grams and moles I use molar mass, and to reach particles I go through moles.
Hand out the first problem set before students leave, tell them it is due at the start of next class, and give them a copy of the periodic table to take home.
Collect the exit half sheets as students leave.
segments.teacherNotes:
Use the half sheets to spot who skips the mole step or inverts the molar mass factor, and plan a short review for them. Remind students the rounded atomic masses on the class table are the ones to use.
Answer key for problem set 1:
1. CaCl₂: 40.08 + 2 × 35.45 = 110.98 g/mol
2. NH₃ is 14.01 + 3 × 1.01 = 17.04 g/mol; 18.0 g × (1 mol / 17.04 g) = 1.06 mol
3. KBr is 39.10 + 79.90 = 119.00 g/mol; 0.425 mol × (119.00 g / 1 mol) = 50.6 g
4. 12.0 g S × (1 mol / 32.06 g) = 0.374 mol; × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol = 2.25 × 10²³ atoms. Size check: a fraction of a mole, and a very large number of atoms.

keyIdeas: Molar mass is the bridge between grams, which we can weigh, and moles, which count particles. To go from grams to moles, divide by the molar mass. To go from moles to grams, multiply by it.
Write the unit with every number and set up each step so the unwanted unit cancels. The setup shows which operation to use.
To go from mass to number of particles, use two steps: grams to moles with molar mass, then moles to particles with 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole. Mass never converts directly to particles.
Check each answer for size. A few grams of a substance is a small fraction of a mole to a few moles, and the number of particles is very large.

study.overview: Molar mass connects the grams you can weigh to the moles that count particles. This guide shows how to convert between grams and moles, and how to go from a mass to a number of atoms or molecules in two steps. Keep the unit with every number and check that each answer is a sensible size.

points.heading: Molar mass converts between grams and moles
points.explanation:
Molar mass is the bridge between grams and moles. To go from grams to moles, divide by the molar mass. To go from moles to grams, multiply by it. Write the unit with every number and set up the factor so the unwanted unit cancels. The unit you want to cancel goes in the denominator, so the setup tells you whether to divide or multiply.

Example: how many moles are in 29.22 g of NaCl? The molar mass is 58.44 g/mol.
29.22 g × (1 mol / 58.44 g) = 0.500 mol
The grams cancel and moles remain.

Reverse example: what is the mass of 2.00 mol of H₂O? The molar mass is 18.02 g/mol.
2.00 mol × (18.02 g / 1 mol) = 36.0 g
Here moles cancel and grams remain. A common mistake is dividing when you should multiply. Check which unit sits on the bottom of your factor.

points.heading: Mass reaches particles in two steps, never one
points.explanation:
Mass never converts directly to a number of particles. Always go through moles. Step 1: grams to moles, using the molar mass. Step 2: moles to particles, using 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole. Skipping the mole step is the most common error.

Example: how many atoms are in a 10.0 g piece of aluminum foil? The molar mass of aluminum is 26.98 g/mol.
10.0 g × (1 mol / 26.98 g) × (6.022 × 10²³ atoms / 1 mol)
Step 1: 10.0 ÷ 26.98 = 0.371 mol
Step 2: 0.371 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.23 × 10²³ atoms
Keep the unrounded calculator value between steps. Rounded values shown in the middle are for display only. Give final answers to three significant figures.

points.heading: Going backward: particles to mass
points.explanation:
The same two steps work in reverse. Divide the number of particles by 6.022 × 10²³ to get moles. Then multiply by the molar mass to get grams. Moles appear in the middle of every chain, whichever direction you go.

Example: what is the mass of 1.20 × 10²⁴ magnesium atoms? The molar mass of magnesium is 24.31 g/mol.
Step 1: 1.20 × 10²⁴ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.99 mol
Step 2: 1.99 × 24.31 = 48.4 g
Write the full unit chain before you touch the calculator. When you enter exponents, type them carefully, because retyping them wrongly is a frequent slip.

points.heading: Check that your answer is a sensible size
points.explanation:
A few grams of a substance is a small fraction of a mole to a few moles. The number of particles in that amount is very large, on the order of 10²² to 10²⁴.

Example: 4.00 g of NaHCO₃ with a molar mass of 84.01 g/mol gives 4.00 ÷ 84.01 = 0.0476 mol. That is a small fraction of a mole, which fits a few grams of a substance. If you had found 336 mol, you would know you multiplied when you should have divided. For particles, an answer such as 2.23 × 10²³ atoms for 10.0 g of aluminum is large, as it should be. Always find the molar mass first, then check that your units cancel.

l_55d7822df40d.title: Balancing chemical equations
l_55d7822df40d.summary: Students use the law of conservation of mass to balance equations, such as H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, by adjusting coefficients.

segments.title: Is this equation true?
segments.description:
Return last time’s exit half sheets and collect the problem set from last time.
Write H₂ + O₂ → H₂O on the board.
Pairs count the atoms of each element on the left and on the right.
Ask: if atoms cannot disappear, what is wrong with this equation?
segments.teacherNotes: Left: 2 H, 2 O. Right: 2 H, 1 O. One oxygen atom seems to vanish. Use the half sheets to seat students who still skip the mole step beside a confident partner.

segments.title: Conservation of mass and coefficients
segments.description:
Introduce the law of conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged in a reaction, never lost or made.
Name the reactants (left of the arrow) and the products (right of the arrow).
Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O with an atom tally table, adjusting one coefficient at a time and recounting.
Show that 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 4 H and 2 O on each side.
Ask why we cannot write H₂O₂ to fix the oxygen count.
segments.teacherNotes: Steps: 2H₂O gives 4 H, 2 O; then 2H₂ fixes hydrogen. Misconception: changing subscripts. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance from water. A coefficient multiplies the whole formula: 2H₂O means 4 H and 2 O.

segments.title: Balancing with a strategy
segments.description:
Model Al + CuCl₂ → AlCl₃ + Cu, the reaction of the second lab later in the course.
Balance chlorine first with a common multiple of 2 and 3, then aluminum, then copper.
Students call out the new coefficient and the recount at each step.
Point out the strategy: tally, change one coefficient, recount, and last of all balance a lone element.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. Cl: 6 on each side. Common mistake: balancing Cl by changing the subscript. Students need not use fractions; double everything if one appears.

segments.title: Balance five equations in pairs
segments.description:
Pairs balance five equations, writing an atom tally for each.
After the second and fourth equations, pairs compare coefficients with a neighboring pair and recount any difference.
The teacher circulates and checks that only coefficients change.
Pairs that finish early explain to each other which element they balanced last, and why.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Mg + O₂ → MgO: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
2. N₂ + H₂ → NH₃: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
3. CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
4. Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃
5. C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
Paper work only; no flames. Twelve minutes is tight for five equations with tallies. If pairs fall behind, make item 5 a challenge for early finishers and be sure every pair finishes item 4.

segments.title: Does the mass balance too?
segments.description:
Return to 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Using molar masses from earlier in the course, students find the mass of 2 mol H₂ and of 1 mol O₂, add them, and compare with the mass of 2 mol H₂O.
Ask: how does the equal mass show that atoms are conserved?
Collect the class’s explanation in one sentence on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2 × 2.02 = 4.04 g; 1 × 32.00 = 32.00 g; total 36.04 g. 2 × 18.02 = 36.04 g. Equal mass on both sides. Do not teach mole ratios yet; ratios of coefficients give mole ratios, which students will use next time.

segments.title: Two-question exit check
segments.description:
Students answer two questions on a half sheet, alone and without notes.
Then the class checks the answers together by a show of hands.
segments.teacherNotes:
Not graded. Q1: Balance Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃. Show your atom tally. Answer: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ (4 Al and 6 O on each side).
Q2: A student balances H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂O₂. In one sentence, say why this is not allowed. Answer: changing a subscript makes a different substance; only coefficients may change.
Use the sheets to spot subscript changes.

segments.title: Summing up balancing
segments.description:
Students finish the sentence aloud in unison: atoms are never lost, so a balanced equation has the same atoms on both sides, and I change only coefficients to get there.
Preview next time: students will read the coefficients as mole ratios.
Collect the half sheets as students leave.
segments.teacherNotes: No homework is set. Plan a short review for students who changed subscripts or stopped after one pass without recounting.

keyIdeas: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms. It does not create or destroy them, so the mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products. This is the law of conservation of mass.
A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.
To balance an equation, change only the coefficients, the whole numbers in front of formulas. Never change a subscript, because that changes the substance.

Work in steps: count the atoms of each element on both sides, adjust one coefficient, and recount. Balance elements that appear in only one compound on each side first, and leave a lone element for last.
Use the smallest whole-number coefficients that balance the equation.

A substance that is made in a reaction. Products are written on the right of the arrow.
A whole number written in front of a formula to show how many of that particle take part. It multiplies every atom in the formula.

study.overview: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms. It never creates or destroys them. This is the law of conservation of mass, and it is why every chemical equation must be balanced: the same number of each kind of atom has to appear on both sides of the arrow. In this lesson you balanced equations by changing coefficients, and you checked that the mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products.

points.heading: Atoms are conserved, so equations must balance
points.explanation: The reactants are on the left of the arrow and the products are on the right. Atoms are rearranged between them, never lost or made, so the mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products. Look at H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. The left side has 2 H and 2 O. The right side has 2 H and 1 O. One oxygen atom seems to vanish, which cannot happen. The equation is not balanced. You checked the mass too, using the balanced equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Two moles of H₂ have a mass of 2 × 2.02 = 4.04 g. One mole of O₂ has a mass of 1 × 32.00 = 32.00 g. Together that is 36.04 g. Two moles of H₂O have a mass of 2 × 18.02 = 36.04 g. The masses are equal, which shows that no atoms were lost.

points.heading: Change only coefficients, never subscripts
points.explanation: A coefficient is the whole number in front of a formula. It multiplies the whole formula: 2H₂O means 4 H and 2 O. A subscript is part of the substance’s identity. If you change H₂O to H₂O₂ to fix the oxygen count, you have written hydrogen peroxide, which is a different substance from water. So the only way to balance an equation is to change coefficients. For H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, put a 2 in front of H₂O to get 4 H and 2 O on the right. Then put a 2 in front of H₂ to match the 4 H. The result is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, with 4 H and 2 O on each side.

points.heading: Balance in steps: tally, change one coefficient, recount
points.explanation: Count the atoms of each element on both sides, often in a tally table. Change one coefficient, then recount. Balance elements that appear in only one compound on each side first, and leave a lone element for last. Try Al + CuCl₂ → AlCl₃ + Cu. Chlorine is 2 on the left and 3 on the right. The common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so write 3CuCl₂ and 2AlCl₃. Now Cl is 6 on each side. Then balance aluminum with 2Al, and copper with 3Cu. The result is 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. If a fraction appears, double every coefficient so that all of them are whole numbers. Use the smallest whole numbers that balance the equation. Always recount at the end, because stopping after one pass can leave an error.

points.heading: Check your answer with a tally
points.explanation: A balanced equation passes a recount: every element has the same total on both sides. Here is the first practice equation worked in full: Mg + O₂ → MgO is not balanced as written, because it has 2 O on the left and 1 O on the right. Writing 2MgO fixes oxygen but makes 2 Mg on the right, so write 2Mg on the left. The result is 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, with 2 Mg and 2 O on each side. Next time you will read these coefficients as mole ratios.

l_5a70eeba95af.title: Mole ratios from balanced equations
l_5a70eeba95af.summary: Students read coefficients as mole ratios and use them to convert moles of one substance to moles of another. The second problem set is set.

segments.title: Balance it, then read it
segments.description:
Return last time’s exit half sheets.
Write Na + Cl₂ → NaCl on the board. Students balance it alone with an atom tally, then compare with a partner.
Ask: if we have 2 Na atoms, how many Cl₂ molecules do they need?
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, so 2 Na for each Cl₂. Common mistake: writing NaCl₂. Use the half sheets to pair students who changed subscripts last time with a partner who did not.

segments.title: Coefficients are mole ratios
segments.description:
Write 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Remind students that last time they found the mass of 2 mol H₂, 1 mol O₂ and 2 mol H₂O.
Read the equation as moles: 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ and make 2 mol H₂O.
Introduce the mole ratio and write three from this equation, each as a fraction. Flip one fraction and show that both forms are true.
Repeat with N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ and have students write the ratio of H₂ to NH₃ themselves.
segments.teacherNotes: Ratios: 2 mol H₂ / 1 mol O₂; 2 mol H₂O / 2 mol H₂; 1 mol O₂ / 2 mol H₂O. H₂ to NH₃ is 3 mol H₂ / 2 mol NH₃. Stress that a ratio uses the coefficient, never the subscript. A missing coefficient means 1.

segments.title: From moles of one substance to moles of another
segments.description:
Pose the question: how many moles of water form from 3.00 mol O₂ in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O?
Work it as a setup: 3.00 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂). Point out that mol O₂ cancels and mol H₂O remains.
Students say aloud which substance goes on the bottom of the ratio before each setup.
Work N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ with 1.50 mol N₂ to find the moles of H₂ needed.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 3.00 × 2 = 6.00 mol H₂O; 1.50 × 3 = 4.50 mol H₂. Common mistake: inverting the ratio. Check that the answer is bigger or smaller as the coefficients predict. Keep three significant figures, as before.

segments.title: Mole-to-mole problems in pairs
segments.description:
Pairs work five problems. For each they write the mole ratio, then the full unit setup, then the answer.
After the third problem, pairs swap papers with a neighboring pair and compare answers.
The teacher circulates and checks that the unwanted unit cancels in every setup.
Pairs that finish early explain to each other how they chose which coefficient went on top.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: write the ratio of NH₃ to H₂. 2 mol NH₃ / 3 mol H₂
2. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 0.600 mol N₂ makes how many mol NH₃? 1.20 mol
3. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: 3.00 mol CH₄ needs how many mol O₂? 6.00 mol
4. C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O: 0.500 mol C₃H₈ makes how many mol CO₂? 1.50 mol
5. 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: 2.40 mol Fe₂O₃ needs how many mol O₂? 3.60 mol

segments.title: Can we use coefficients for grams?
segments.description:
Write on the board a student’s claim: in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 g of H₂ react with 1 g of O₂, because the coefficients are 2 and 1.
Students decide in pairs whether it is true, using the masses they found last time.
Collect one sentence on the board that says what the coefficients count.
segments.teacherNotes: Not true: 2 mol H₂ is 4.04 g and 1 mol O₂ is 32.00 g. Coefficients count moles, so mass must go through moles first. Expected sentence: coefficients give ratios of moles, not grams.

segments.title: Two-question exit check
segments.description:
Students answer two questions on a half sheet, alone and without notes.
The class then checks the answers together by a show of hands.
Collect the half sheets as students leave.
segments.teacherNotes:
Not graded.
Q1: 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O. How many moles of O₂ react with 0.800 mol C₂H₂? Show your setup. Answer: 0.800 × 5/2 = 2.00 mol O₂.
Q2: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. How many moles of O₂ form from 1.50 mol KClO₃? Answer: 1.50 × 3/2 = 2.25 mol O₂.
Use the sheets to spot inverted ratios.

segments.title: Summing up and homework
segments.description:
Students finish the sentence aloud in unison: the coefficients give the mole ratio, and I put the moles I want on top.
Preview next time: students will use mole ratios in a lab with baking soda and vinegar.
Hand out the second problem set before students leave. Tell them it is due at the start of next class and that they need the periodic table they took home.
segments.teacherNotes:
Remind students to show unit setups and use the rounded atomic masses on the class table.
Answer key for problem set 2:
1. 2 mol AlCl₃ / 3 mol Cl₂
2. 0.625 mol CaCO₃ × (1 mol CO₂ / 1 mol CaCO₃) = 0.625 mol CO₂
3. 1.20 mol O₂ × (2 mol MgO / 1 mol O₂) = 2.40 mol MgO
4. 13.5 g Al × (1 mol / 26.98 g) = 0.500 mol Al; × (3 mol O₂ / 4 mol Al) = 0.375 mol O₂
 Plan a short review for students who inverted ratios or used subscripts instead of coefficients.

keyIdeas: The coefficients in a balanced equation give the ratio of moles of each substance. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ and make 2 mol H₂O.
A mole ratio is a conversion factor. Put the moles of the substance you want on top and the moles of the substance you have on the bottom, so the unit you have cancels.
To convert moles of A to moles of B, use the coefficients of A and B only. For example, 3.00 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂) = 6.00 mol H₂O.
Coefficients give ratios of moles, not ratios of grams. Convert mass to moles first, because balanced equations count particles, not mass.

vocabulary.definition: The ratio of moles of two substances in a balanced equation, taken from their coefficients, such as 2 mol H₂ to 1 mol O₂.
Using balanced equations and mole ratios to calculate the amounts of reactants and products in a reaction.

study.overview: The coefficients in a balanced equation tell you how many moles of each substance take part in a reaction. This lets you turn moles of one substance into moles of another. Read the equation as a recipe in moles, write the right mole ratio as a fraction, and let the units cancel. Coefficients never count grams, so mass must be converted to moles first.

points.heading: Coefficients are mole ratios
points.explanation: In a balanced equation, the coefficients give the ratio of moles of each substance. A missing coefficient means 1. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ and make 2 mol H₂O. From this you can write mole ratios as fractions, such as 2 mol H₂ / 1 mol O₂ or 2 mol H₂O / 2 mol H₂. Flip a fraction and it is still true: 1 mol O₂ / 2 mol H₂ describes the same relationship. Always use the coefficient, never the subscript. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the ratio of H₂ to NH₃ is 3 mol H₂ / 2 mol NH₃. The subscript 2 in H₂ is not part of the ratio.

points.heading: Use a mole ratio as a conversion factor
points.explanation: To convert moles of A to moles of B, put the moles of the substance you want on top and the moles of the substance you have on the bottom. Then the unit you have cancels. Use the coefficients of A and B only. Example: how many moles of water form from 3.00 mol O₂ in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O? Write 3.00 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂) = 6.00 mol H₂O. The mol O₂ cancels and mol H₂O remains. Another example: in N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 1.50 mol N₂ needs 1.50 mol N₂ × (3 mol H₂ / 1 mol N₂) = 4.50 mol H₂. Before you start, say aloud which substance goes on the bottom.

points.heading: Check for inverted ratios
points.explanation: The most common mistake is turning the ratio upside down. A quick check helps. Look at the coefficients and predict whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the number you started with. In the O₂ to H₂O example, water has the larger coefficient (2 versus 1), so the answer, 6.00 mol, should be larger than 3.00 mol. It is. If your answer goes the wrong way, flip the ratio. Also check that the unwanted unit cancels in your setup, and keep three significant figures.

points.heading: Coefficients are not grams
points.explanation: Someone might claim that in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 g of H₂ react with 1 g of O₂ because the coefficients are 2 and 1. That is not true. 2 mol H₂ has a mass of 4.04 g, and 1 mol O₂ has a mass of 32.00 g. Balanced equations count particles, not mass. So the coefficients give ratios of moles, not ratios of grams. If you are given a mass, convert it to moles first, then use the mole ratio.

l_b08492b9239c.title: Lab: mass of carbon dioxide from baking soda and vinegar
l_b08492b9239c.summary: Students react baking soda with vinegar, find the CO₂ released from the mass lost, and compare it with the predicted value. The lab report is set.

segments.title: Conservation of mass, then a puzzle
segments.description:
Return last time’s exit half sheets and collect the problem set from last time.
Write NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ on the board. Pairs count the atoms on each side and agree that it is balanced.
Ask: if mass is conserved, why would a cup of fizzing vinegar get lighter on a balance?
segments.teacherNotes: Atoms: NaHCO₃ contributes 1 C and CH₃COOH contributes 2 C, giving 3 C on the left; check each element: Na 1, C 3, H 5, O 5 on both sides. Expected answer: CO₂ gas leaves the cup.

segments.title: Finding CO₂ from a mass difference
segments.description:
Explain that both weighings include the same cup and weigh boat, with all the reactants included before mixing and all remaining material afterward. If nothing spills and evaporation is small, the mass lost estimates the mass of CO₂ released.
Model the method with a different reaction: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, using 2.50 g CaCO₃. Convert 2.50 g to moles, use the coefficients to get moles of CO₂, then convert to grams.
Show the two weighings: a starting mass with the boat and a final mass with the same boat. Students say which mass is the CO₂.
Walk through the lab steps on the board, then ask students to name the readings they must write down.
segments.teacherNotes: Model answer: 2.50 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.0250 mol CaCO₃; ratio 1 : 1; 0.0250 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 1.10 g CO₂. Misconception: mass lost equals mass of soda. Readings: empty boat, boat with soda, starting total, final total with the boat. Use the class table’s rounded masses.

segments.title: Weigh the baking soda and predict the CO₂
segments.description:
Pairs put on goggles and aprons, then weigh the empty weigh boat and record it. They add about 2 g of baking soda, weigh the boat again, and find the mass of baking soda by subtraction.
Before any vinegar is added, pairs predict the mass of CO₂. They convert grams of NaHCO₃ to moles, use the 1 : 1 ratio, and convert to grams of CO₂.
The teacher checks each prediction against the data sheet before a pair moves on.
segments.teacherNotes:
Molar masses: NaHCO₃ 84.01 g/mol, CO₂ 44.01 g/mol. Check: 2.00 g gives about 1.05 g CO₂, but pairs have their own masses; the prediction is the baking soda mass × 0.524.
Prep for 14 pairs: 1 L of 5% white vinegar (700 mL is used), a 250 g box of baking soda (about 30 g is used), 14 clear plastic cups of at least 250 mL with a 50 mL line marked on each, 14 weigh boats, 14 spatulas or spoons, paper towels, and a data sheet for every student. Balances must read to 0.01 g; four or more keep the line short.
Safety: goggles and apron on for all handling; hair tied back; keep the balance dry; no tasting or eating anything in the lab. Baking soda and vinegar are mild, but both sting the eyes. For a splash in the eye, rinse at the eyewash station for several minutes and tell the teacher.

segments.title: Lab: react baking soda with vinegar
segments.description:
Each pair pours about 50 mL of vinegar into a large plastic cup. They place the cup and the boat holding the baking soda on the balance together and record the starting mass.
They take both off, tip the baking soda slowly into the vinegar, tap the boat empty, and brush any left-over powder into the cup. Then they put the cup and the same boat back on the balance.
They wait until the fizzing stops and the reading settles, then record the final mass. Pairs clean up and wash hands.
segments.teacherNotes: The final mass must include the boat, or its mass counts as lost CO₂. Cup and boat go on the pan together both times. Dry their outsides before the starting weighing. If reaction liquid spills or must be wiped away afterward, record the loss and repeat with fresh materials. Before the final weighing, have pairs swirl the cup gently, off the balance, until no new bubbles rise, so that less CO₂ stays dissolved. Safety: goggles and apron; 5% vinegar is mild but stings eyes, so rinse a splash at the eyewash station for several minutes; never taste it; add soda slowly as the foam can overflow; mop spills at once; pour liquid down the sink with running water; wash hands.

segments.title: Measured against predicted CO₂
segments.description:
Pairs subtract the final mass from the starting mass to get the measured mass of CO₂. They compare it with their prediction and write the difference in grams.
Each pair writes its prediction and measured value on the board.
The class looks for a pattern. Ask: why might the measured mass be smaller or larger than predicted, and which reasons fit what we did?
segments.teacherNotes: Expect most pairs to measure 0.05 to 0.15 g less than they predicted. A value above the prediction usually means liquid was lost. Likely reasons: some CO₂ stays dissolved in the liquid; powder left in the boat; foam sprayed out; balance not settled; small mass of water vapor carried off with the gas. Students use their own data for the report; do not hand back an answer key.

segments.title: Wrap-up and report assignment
segments.description:
Students finish aloud: the mass lost is the CO₂, and I compare it with the prediction from the mole ratio.
Before students leave, set the lab report and give its due date.
Each student takes home their own data sheet and a periodic table. Preview next time: the class will keep using mole ratios with masses.
segments.teacherNotes:
Check that every pair has the boat’s empty mass, boat and soda mass, starting total, and final total on their data sheet before they leave. Prepare a data sheet for each student in advance, and have both partners record every reading so each can take the measured data home. Remind students to bring only their own measured values to the report. Students keep the data sheet and bring it back: the next lesson opens with it, and it is the fallback data in the percent yield lesson.
Marking check for the reports: predicted CO₂ = mass of baking soda × 44.01 ÷ 84.01, which is the mass × 0.524.

keyIdeas: When baking soda reacts with vinegar, one product is carbon dioxide gas. It escapes into the air, so the mass left on the balance goes down. The mass lost is the mass of CO₂ released.

Everything must stay on the balance for the mass difference to mean CO₂ only. Weigh the cup, the vinegar and the weigh boat holding the baking soda before the reaction, and weigh the same cup, the same liquid and the same boat after it.

The mass of baking soda used is the mass of the boat with baking soda minus the mass of the empty boat. Predict CO₂ by converting that mass to moles of NaHCO₃, using the 1 : 1 mole ratio to get moles of CO₂, and converting to grams.
Measured and predicted CO₂ will rarely match exactly. Compare them by their difference in grams, then give reasons for it that fit the procedure and the direction of the difference.

vocabulary.definition: The starting mass of a system minus its final mass. In this lab it equals the mass of CO₂ gas that escaped.

study.overview: In this lab you reacted baking soda (NaHCO₃) with vinegar and found the carbon dioxide released by weighing. CO₂ is a gas and escapes into the air, so the mass on the balance goes down. This guide shows how to measure that loss, how to predict the CO₂ from a mole ratio, and how to compare the two values. Use your own measured data for the lab report.

points.heading: The mass lost is the mass of CO₂
points.explanation: In NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂, one product is a gas. It leaves the cup, so the balance reading drops even though mass is conserved: the missing mass is in the air as CO₂. Subtract the final mass from the starting mass: measured CO₂ = starting mass − final mass. Example: if a starting total were 150.00 g and the final total were 149.00 g, the measured CO₂ would be 1.00 g. Note that this is the mass of gas that escaped, not the mass of baking soda you used.

points.heading: Keep everything on the balance
points.explanation: The mass difference only means CO₂ if nothing else is gained or lost. Weigh the cup, the vinegar and the weigh boat holding the baking soda before mixing. After the reaction, weigh the same cup, the same liquid and the same boat. The boat must be included both times. If you left it out the second time, its mass would wrongly count as lost CO₂. Also dry the outside of the cup and boat before the first weighing, and wait until the fizzing stops and the reading settles before you record the final mass.

points.heading: Predict the CO₂ with the mole ratio
points.explanation: First find the mass of baking soda: mass of boat with soda − mass of empty boat. Then convert to moles, use the 1 : 1 ratio, and convert to grams of CO₂. Worked example with a different reaction, CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, using 2.50 g CaCO₃: 2.50 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.0250 mol CaCO₃. The ratio of CaCO₃ to CO₂ is 1 : 1, so there is 0.0250 mol CO₂. Then 0.0250 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 1.10 g CO₂. For baking soda, use 84.01 g/mol for NaHCO₃ and 44.01 g/mol for CO₂, with your own masses.

points.heading: Compare measured and predicted values
points.explanation: Measured and predicted CO₂ will rarely match exactly. Compare them by writing the difference in grams, and note which value is larger. Then look for reasons in what you actually did. Ask yourself three questions. Did all the CO₂ that formed leave the cup? Did anything other than CO₂ leave the cup? Did all the baking soda you weighed end up in the vinegar? For each answer, work out whether it would make your measured CO₂ higher or lower than the prediction, and check that the direction matches your result. Choose the reasons that fit your own procedure, and use only your own measured values in your report.

segments.title: The chain you used last time
segments.description:
Pairs look at their lab data sheets from last time.
They list, in order, the conversions they used to get from grams of baking soda to grams of CO₂.
Write the list on the board as four boxes: grams NaHCO₃, moles NaHCO₃, moles CO₂, grams CO₂.
Ask: which arrow used the coefficients?
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: the middle arrow, with a 1 : 1 ratio. The outer arrows use 84.01 g/mol and 44.01 g/mol. Pairs use their own numbers. Say that the lab prediction was already a mass-to-mass problem, so today names and extends it.

segments.title: Three-step conversion: grams to grams
segments.description:
Write N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ and ask: how many grams of NH₃ form from 14.0 g N₂ when H₂ is in excess?
Build the setup as three fractions in one line, with the unit you do not want crossed out at each step.
Label the steps: grams to moles, mole ratio, moles to grams.
Students copy the setup and say aloud which unit cancels at each step.
segments.teacherNotes: Use N 14.01, H 1.01. 14.0 ÷ 28.02 = 0.500 mol N₂; × 2/1 = 0.999 mol NH₃; × 17.04 g/mol = 17.0 g. The calculator holds 0.4996 for the first step, so doubling it gives 0.999, not 1.00: keep the calculator value between steps and round only what is written down. Common mistakes: skipping the first step, or using coefficients as grams. Keep three significant figures.

segments.title: Mass-to-mass problems in pairs
segments.description:
Pairs solve three mass-to-mass problems. For each problem, state that the other reactant is in excess.
For each one they write the four-box chain first, then the full unit setup, then the answer.
The teacher circulates and checks that the mole ratio comes from the coefficients of the two substances only.
Pairs that finish early check each other’s unit cancellations.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: grams of CO₂ from 8.00 g CH₄? 21.9 g
2. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: grams of H₂O from 6.00 g O₂? 6.76 g
3. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: grams of NH₃ from 10.0 g H₂? 56.2 g
Watch for an inverted ratio in item 3.

segments.title: Which reactant runs out first?
segments.description:
Start with a hypothetical bike shop: each bike needs 2 wheels and 1 frame, and the shop has 10 wheels and 8 frames.
Students decide how many bikes can be built and what runs out first.
Then use 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 4.00 g H₂ and 16.00 g O₂.
For each reactant, find the moles of water it could make. The smaller amount names the limiting reactant. Then find how much of the other reactant is left over.
segments.teacherNotes: Bikes: 5 bikes, wheels limit, 3 frames left. H₂: 1.98 mol, could make 1.98 mol water. O₂: 0.500 mol, could make 1.00 mol water (18.0 g). O₂ limits. H₂ used: 1.00 mol; left 0.980 mol, 1.98 g. Misconception: the smaller mass limits. Here H₂ has less mass but is in excess.

segments.title: Find the limiting reactant and the excess
segments.description:
Pairs work three problems.
For each, they find the moles of product from each reactant, name the limiting reactant, and find the moles of the excess reactant left over.
Pairs write their answers on a half sheet and compare with a neighboring pair.
The teacher asks any pair with a different answer to find the first step where the two solutions differ.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers (moles of product from each reactant in brackets):
1. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 14.0 g N₂, 2.00 g H₂. H₂ limits (0.660 mol vs 0.999 mol NH₃); 0.170 mol N₂ left.
2. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: 4.00 g CH₄, 4.00 g O₂. O₂ limits (0.0625 mol vs 0.249 mol CO₂); 0.187 mol CH₄ left.
3. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: 3.00 g Mg, 4.00 g O₂. Mg limits (0.123 mol vs 0.250 mol MgO); 0.0633 mol O₂ left.

segments.title: Two-question exit check
segments.description:
Students answer two questions on a half sheet, alone and without notes.
The class checks the answers together by a show of hands.
Collect the half sheets as students leave.
segments.teacherNotes:
Not graded. Use the sheets to plan a short review.
Q1: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. How many grams of NaCl form from 4.60 g Na when Cl₂ is in excess? Show your setup. Answer: 4.60 ÷ 22.99 = 0.200 mol Na; × 2/2; × 58.44 = 11.7 g.
Q2: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Which is limiting, 4.60 g Na or 3.55 g Cl₂? Answer: Cl₂. 3.55 ÷ 70.90 = 0.0501 mol Cl₂ could make 0.100 mol NaCl; 0.200 mol Na could make 0.200 mol NaCl.

segments.title: Sum up and set the problem set
segments.description:
Students finish aloud: I change grams to moles, compare what each reactant can make, and the smaller amount is the limiting reactant.
Preview next time: the class will use a limiting reactant in a lab with copper chloride and aluminum foil.
Hand out the third problem set before students leave. Tell them it is due at the start of next class and that they need the periodic table they took home.
segments.teacherNotes:
Remind students to show unit setups, use the rounded atomic masses on the class table, and give final answers to three significant figures. Next time is a lab day: closed-toe shoes, and long hair tied back. Plan a short review for students who compared grams instead of moles.
Answer key for problem set 3:
1. KBr is 39.10 + 79.90 = 119.00 g/mol. 6.50 g K × (1 mol / 39.10 g) = 0.166 mol K; × (2 mol KBr / 2 mol K) = 0.166 mol KBr; × (119.00 g / 1 mol) = 19.8 g KBr
2. Al: 5.40 g ÷ 26.98 g/mol = 0.200 mol; × 2/2 = 0.200 mol Fe. Fe₂O₃ is 159.70 g/mol: 8.00 g ÷ 159.70 g/mol = 0.0501 mol; × 2/1 = 0.100 mol Fe. Fe₂O₃ is limiting.
3. 0.100 mol Fe forms. It uses up 0.100 mol Al, so 0.200 − 0.100 = 0.100 mol Al is left.
4. C₃H₈ is 44.11 g/mol: 10.0 g ÷ 44.11 g/mol = 0.227 mol, which could make 0.680 mol CO₂. O₂: 32.0 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 1.00 mol, which could make 0.600 mol CO₂. O₂ is limiting. C₃H₈ used: 1.00 mol O₂ × 1/5 = 0.200 mol; left: 0.2267 − 0.2000 = 0.0267 mol. CO₂: 0.600 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 26.4 g

keyIdeas: A mass-to-mass problem is a three-step chain: grams of the substance you have → moles of it (divide by its molar mass), moles of it → moles of the substance you want (mole ratio from the coefficients), moles of the wanted substance → grams (multiply by its molar mass).
The mole ratio is the only step that uses coefficients. The two molar-mass steps use the masses from the periodic table.

The limiting reactant is the reactant that runs out first, so it decides how much product forms. To find it, work out how much product each reactant could make. The smaller amount belongs to the limiting reactant.
The reactant that is not limiting is in excess, and some is left over. Find how much reacted using the mole ratio, then subtract it from the amount you started with.
The reactant with the smaller mass is not always the limiting reactant. Compare moles and coefficients, not grams.

vocabulary.definition: The reactant that is used up first in a reaction. It decides how much product can form.
The reactant that is not used up. Some of it is left over after the limiting reactant runs out.

study.overview: Today you learned to solve mass-to-mass problems and to find the limiting reactant. A mass-to-mass problem is a three-step chain: grams to moles, moles to moles, then moles to grams. The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it decides how much product forms. The reactant that is not limiting is in excess, and some is left over. Use this guide to review the method and the worked examples. On the third problem set, show your unit setups and use the rounded atomic masses on the class periodic table.

points.heading: Mass-to-mass problems use a three-step chain
points.explanation:
Every mass-to-mass problem follows four boxes: grams of the substance you have, moles of it, moles of the substance you want, grams of the substance you want. Step 1: divide by the molar mass of the substance you have. Step 2: multiply by the mole ratio. Step 3: multiply by the molar mass of the substance you want. Cross out the unit you do not want at each step.

Example: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. How many grams of NH₃ form from 14.0 g N₂ when H₂ is in excess? Use N 14.01 and H 1.01. First, 14.0 g ÷ 28.02 g/mol = 0.4996 mol N₂, which you write as 0.500 mol. Next, × 2/1 = 0.999 mol NH₃. Last, × 17.04 g/mol = 17.0 g NH₃. Keep the calculator value between steps, and round only the numbers you write down, to three significant figures. Common mistakes are skipping the first step and using coefficients as grams.

points.heading: Only the mole ratio uses the coefficients
points.explanation:
The middle step is the only one that uses the coefficients of the balanced equation. The two outer steps use molar masses from the periodic table. Take the ratio from the coefficients of the two substances in the problem only, and put the wanted substance on top.

Example: in the lab last time, you went from grams of NaHCO₃ to grams of CO₂. The outer arrows used 84.01 g/mol and 44.01 g/mol. The middle arrow used a 1 : 1 ratio. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, going from H₂ to NH₃ uses 2/3, not 3/2. Check that your ratio is not upside down: it is easy to invert it.

points.heading: The limiting reactant makes the smallest amount of product
points.explanation:
To find the limiting reactant, change the grams of each reactant to moles. Then work out how many moles of product each one could make. The smaller amount belongs to the limiting reactant. The other reactant is in excess. To find how much is left, use the mole ratio to find how much reacted, then subtract it from the amount you started with.

Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 4.00 g H₂ and 16.00 g O₂. H₂: 4.00 ÷ 2.02 = 1.98 mol, which could make 1.98 mol water. O₂: 16.00 ÷ 32.00 = 0.500 mol, which could make 1.00 mol water (18.0 g). O₂ gives the smaller amount, so O₂ is limiting. H₂ used: 1.00 mol. H₂ left: 1.98 − 1.00 = 0.980 mol, which is 1.98 g.

points.heading: Compare moles and coefficients, not grams
points.explanation:
It is tempting to think the reactant with the smaller mass must be limiting. That is not always true. Grams do not tell you how many particles you have, and the equation counts particles.

In the water example above, H₂ has less mass (4.00 g) than O₂ (16.00 g). Yet H₂ is in excess, because its moles are larger and the equation needs only 2 H₂ for every 1 O₂. A simple picture: a shop makes bikes from 2 wheels and 1 frame each. With 10 wheels and 8 frames, the wheels run out after 5 bikes, so wheels limit and 3 frames are left. Always compare what each reactant can make, in moles of product.

l_adc5c27d3a0b.title: Lab: limiting reactant with copper chloride and aluminum foil
l_adc5c27d3a0b.summary: Students react copper(II) chloride solution with aluminum foil, 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu, to find the limiting reactant. The lab report is set.

segments.title: Balance the equation, then predict what you will see
segments.description:
Return last time’s exit half sheets and collect the third problem set. Write 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu on the board, and pairs count the atoms on each side.
Pairs then write what they would see if the aluminum runs out first, and what they would see if the copper(II) chloride runs out first.
Take two or three answers aloud.
segments.teacherNotes: Atoms: Al 2, Cu 3, Cl 6 on both sides. Expected: aluminum runs out, so the foil is gone and the solution stays blue. Copper(II) chloride runs out, so the blue fades and foil is left. Accept ‘color change’ as a partial answer and ask which color.

segments.title: Model the prediction and walk through the lab
segments.description:
Model a prediction with different masses: 0.80 g Al and 3.00 g CuCl₂·2H₂O. Change each mass to moles, use the coefficients to find the moles of Cu each could make, and name the limiting reactant.
Explain that the blue solid is the dihydrate, so 1 mol of it gives 1 mol of CuCl₂. Its molar mass is 170.5 g/mol.
Walk through the steps on the board: weigh the filter paper, the foil and the salt, predict, react, observe, then recover the copper.
Point out the two setups on the bench. Pairs will be given one of them and will pool results afterward.
segments.teacherNotes: Model: 0.80 ÷ 26.98 = 0.0297 mol Al, × 3/2 = 0.0445 mol Cu. 3.00 ÷ 170.5 = 0.0176 mol salt, × 3/3 = 0.0176 mol Cu. CuCl₂ limits; 1.12 g Cu; 0.48 g Al left. Misconception: smaller mass limits. Use Cu 63.55.

segments.title: Weigh the reactants and predict the limiting reactant
segments.description:
Pairs put on goggles, aprons and gloves. They weigh a labeled filter paper and record its mass. They weigh their foil piece, copy the mass of copper(II) chloride written on their cup, and dissolve the salt in 40 mL of water in a 250 mL beaker.
Before any foil goes in, they calculate the moles of Cu each reactant could make. They name the limiting reactant and predict the grams of copper.
The teacher checks each prediction against the data sheet before a pair moves on.
segments.teacherNotes:
Setup A (seven pairs): about 0.25 g foil, 3.40 g salt. Al limits (0.0139 mol Cu vs 0.0199 mol); about 0.88 g Cu. Setup B (seven pairs): about 0.50 g foil, 1.70 g salt. CuCl₂ limits (0.00997 mol vs 0.0278 mol); about 0.63 g Cu. Pairs use their own masses. Quick check: when Al limits, predicted copper is the foil mass × 3.53; when CuCl₂ limits, it is the salt mass × 0.373.
Prep for 14 pairs: 40 g of CuCl₂·2H₂O (the pairs use 35.7 g; the rest is for your trial runs). Weigh it into 14 labeled cups, seven of 3.40 g and seven of 1.70 g, and write the exact mass on each cup. Cut 14 pieces of regular kitchen foil, about 7 cm × 8 cm for 0.25 g and 8 cm × 14 cm for 0.50 g, and check one of each on a balance. For each pair: a 250 mL beaker, stirring rod, thermometer, tweezers, spatula, funnel, filter paper, a flask to catch the filtrate, a wash bottle of water, a watch glass and a pencil. For the room: balances reading to 0.01 g, 30 pairs of nitrile gloves, 2 L of distilled water, a labeled 2 L bottle for copper solution waste and a labeled tub for solid copper waste. Run one trial of each setup first.
Safety: goggles, apron and nitrile gloves from now until clean-up ends. Copper(II) chloride is harmful if swallowed and irritates skin and eyes, so no tasting and no eating. Show students the eyewash station before they start. For a splash in the eye: go to the eyewash at once, hold the eyelids open, rinse for at least 15 minutes, and send for the school nurse. For a splash on skin: rinse under running water for several minutes. Wash hands after.

segments.title: Lab: react the foil with the solution
segments.description:
Pairs record the color of the solution, loosely crumple the foil, and drop it into the beaker. They stir gently every minute with a stirring rod.
They record observations at the start, after about five minutes, and after about ten minutes. They note the color of the solution, the foil left, any bubbles, the solid that forms, and the thermometer reading.
When the changes stop, each pair writes down whether foil remains and whether the solution is still blue.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expect: foil darkens, reddish-brown copper forms, bubbles appear, beaker warms. Foil may start slowly because of its oxide layer. Crumpling speeds it up. If foil remains and the solution is blue or pale, keep stirring. Setup A should lose its foil; setup B should lose its blue color.
Safety: the reaction gives off a lot of heat. The solution can pass 50 °C within a few minutes, so the beaker stays on the bench, nobody holds it or leans over it, and pairs read the thermometer instead of touching the glass. If a mixture foams up or steams, the pair steps back and calls you. Let the beaker cool for a few minutes before the next step. The bubbles are hydrogen: no flames or sparks, and keep windows open or the room ventilation running. Do not touch the solution. Goggles and gloves stay on.

segments.title: Recover and wash the copper
segments.description:
Pairs lift any leftover foil out with tweezers. They scrape the copper stuck to it into the beaker with a spatula, then rinse the foil over the beaker.
They pour the mixture through the pre-weighed filter paper, then rinse the beaker into the funnel. They wash the copper on the paper three times with about 10 mL of water each time, and let each rinse drain.
They open the paper onto a labeled watch glass and pour the filtrate into the waste container. They clean up and wash their hands.
segments.teacherNotes:
Aluminum is removed before filtering, so the copper is not mixed with it. The rinses remove dissolved salts. Filtering is the slow step: have pairs let the copper settle, pour most of the liquid through the paper first, then wash the copper in. Funnels can finish draining during the discussion. Dry the papers flat on their watch glasses at room temperature until next lesson (at least 24 hours), or in an oven no hotter than 80 °C for about an hour. Before next lesson, test two or three papers for constant mass: weigh, dry for 15 minutes more, and reweigh; the readings should agree within 0.02 g. Next lesson, pairs weigh the paper plus copper once and subtract the paper’s mass.
Safety: all filtrate and rinse water go into the labeled copper waste bottle, never down the drain. Leftover foil goes into the labeled tub for solid copper waste; the copper and filter paper join it after next lesson’s weighing. Hand both containers to the school’s chemical waste collection. Gloves stay on until the bench is wiped down. Wash hands.

segments.title: Confirm the limiting reactant from the observations
segments.description:
Each pair writes its setup, predicted limiting reactant, and what it saw on the class table on the board.
Ask: for each row, do the observations match the prediction? What is the evidence?
Ask: why does aluminum have the smaller mass in both setups, yet limit in only one?
Pairs that see a mismatch name a likely reason that fits what they did.
segments.teacherNotes: Confirmed: foil gone and blue left means Al limited. Blue gone and foil left means CuCl₂ limited. Possible mismatch reasons: reaction not finished, foil oxide layer, weighing slip, wrong mole ratio. Answer: Al’s molar mass is small, so its grams make many moles. Compare moles and coefficients, not grams.

segments.title: Sum up and set the lab report
segments.description:
Students finish aloud: my prediction came from comparing the moles of copper each reactant could make, and my observations test it.
Before students leave, set the lab report on this experiment and give its due date, after next lesson.
Give each student a copy of the recorded data and a periodic table to take home.
Preview next time: the class will weigh the dried copper and compare it with the prediction.
segments.teacherNotes: Check that every student has the filter paper mass, foil mass, salt mass, prediction and observations recorded on the data sheet before leaving, and tell them to bring the sheet next lesson, when pairs weigh the dried copper and add that mass to the report. Make sure each watch glass is labeled with pair initials and left somewhere undisturbed to dry. Marking check for the reports: when Al limits, predicted copper = foil mass × 3.53 (1.5 × 63.55 ÷ 26.98); when CuCl₂ limits, predicted copper = salt mass × 0.373 (63.55 ÷ 170.5).

study.overview: In this lab you reacted aluminum foil with copper(II) chloride solution: 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. One reactant runs out first. That reactant is the limiting reactant, and it decides how much copper can form. You predicted which reactant would limit before the foil went in, then used your observations to check the prediction. Next time you will weigh your dried copper and compare it with your predicted mass.

points.heading: Predict the limiting reactant with moles, not grams
points.explanation: Change the mass of each reactant to moles. Then use the coefficients to find the moles of copper each one could make. The smaller amount of copper belongs to the limiting reactant. Example: suppose 0.80 g Al and 3.00 g CuCl₂·2H₂O. The blue solid is the dihydrate, so 1 mol of it gives 1 mol of CuCl₂. Its molar mass is 170.5 g/mol. Aluminum: 0.80 ÷ 26.98 = 0.0297 mol Al, × 3/2 = 0.0445 mol Cu. Salt: 3.00 ÷ 170.5 = 0.0176 mol, × 3/3 = 0.0176 mol Cu. The salt makes less copper, so CuCl₂ limits. It can make 0.0176 mol × 63.55 g/mol = 1.12 g Cu. About 0.48 g of the aluminum is left over.

points.heading: The smaller mass is not always the limiting reactant
points.explanation: Aluminum had the smaller mass in both lab setups, yet it limited in only one. Grams are not the right thing to compare. Aluminum’s molar mass is small, so a small mass of foil is a lot of moles. Always compare the moles of product each reactant could make, using the coefficients. Look again at the example above: 0.80 g of aluminum is far less mass than 3.00 g of the salt, but the aluminum could make 0.0445 mol Cu and the salt only 0.0176 mol, so the salt limits. Now do the same with the masses on your own data sheet. Your report needs your own numbers and your own working.

points.heading: Use observations to confirm the prediction
points.explanation: Reddish-brown copper forms either way, so the copper alone does not tell you which reactant limited. Look at the foil and the color of the solution. If aluminum is limiting, the foil disappears and the blue color stays. If copper(II) chloride is limiting, the blue color fades and foil is left over. In your report, set what you saw beside what you predicted and say whether they agree. If they do not agree, do not force them to. Go back over two things: your calculation (the masses, the molar masses, the mole ratio) and your procedure (how long the reaction ran, and how the foil behaved at the start). Then say which one you think explains the mismatch, and why.

points.heading: Recover the copper carefully to get a mass you can trust
points.explanation: The copper mass will be compared with your prediction, so each step matters. Weigh the filter paper first. Remove any leftover foil before filtering. Filter the copper, rinse it three times, and let it dry until its mass stops changing. Each step either keeps something else out of the final mass or keeps copper in it. For each step, ask yourself: if we had skipped it, what else would be on the paper, or what copper would be missing? Would the mass read higher or lower? You will need that reasoning when you compare your dried copper with your prediction. Pour all filtrate into the labeled waste bottle, never down the drain.

points.heading: Theoretical yield and actual yield
points.explanation: Theoretical yield is the mass of product a reaction should make if all of the limiting reactant turns into product. You calculate it with the same mass-to-mass chain used earlier in the course, and you must start from the limiting reactant. Actual yield is the mass of product you really collected. It is measured in the lab, sometimes by subtracting measured masses. Example: in Zn + CuCl₂ → ZnCl₂ + Cu with 1.00 g of each reactant, CuCl₂ is the limiting reactant. Theoretical yield: 0.00744 mol CuCl₂ × 1/1 × 63.55 g/mol = 0.473 g Cu. Suppose a student dried and weighed 0.400 g of copper. That 0.400 g is the measured actual yield. The 0.473 g is the calculated theoretical yield. A common mistake is to start from the non-limiting reactant.

points.heading: Calculating percent yield
points.explanation: Percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%. It tells you what share of the possible product you got. Both yields must be in the same unit, such as grams. Always divide actual by theoretical, not the other way around. Example: a student collected 0.400 g of copper when the theoretical yield was 0.473 g. Percent yield = 0.400 ÷ 0.473 × 100% = 84.6%. Another example: the bike shop could build 5 bikes but built 4, so 4 ÷ 5 × 100% = 80%. In your own work, show the formula, the numbers with units, and the answer to three significant figures. If you calculate a value above 100%, something is wrong. You have more than all the product possible, so the product is probably wet or impure.

points.heading: Why percent yield is usually below 100%
points.explanation: Product is often lost or never forms. Two common sources are an incomplete reaction and product lost in handling. In an incomplete reaction, the reaction stops while some reactant is still left, so less product forms. Loss in handling happens when product stays behind, for example solid stuck on glassware or filter paper. Example: if a solid stays stuck on the filter paper and beaker, that is loss in handling. If a reaction is stopped while reactant remains, that is an incomplete reaction. Other reasons you may meet are a side reaction, where some reactant forms a different substance, and gas that dissolves in the liquid and is never measured. When you explain a low yield, name a specific cause like these.
