segments.title: Unit test on stoichiometry
segments.description:
Hand out the test and tell students when it ends.
Students work alone and in silence, showing the formula or setup and the numbers with units. They give final calculated amounts and percent yields to three significant figures, keep molar masses to the precision of the class table, and use the smallest whole-number coefficients when balancing.
The teacher circulates, answers only questions about wording, and gives a time check with ten minutes left.
Collect each paper when time is up, or when a student finishes and has checked their work.
segments.teacherNotes:
Total 40 points. Copy the test paper below for students, leaving working space under each question. The answer key follows it. Atomic masses needed, from the class table: H 1.01, C 12.01, N 14.01, O 16.00, Na 22.99, Cl 35.45, K 39.10, Ca 40.08, Fe 55.85.
Marking: award method points when a wrong earlier value is carried through correctly. Where the key says ‘answer with unit’, withhold that point if the unit is missing; make no other deduction for units. Accept an answer that differs by 1 in the third significant figure because of rounding between steps.

TEST PAPER
Unit test: stoichiometry. Name: ____________ Total: 40 points.
Show every setup with units. Give molar masses to two decimal places and other final answers to three significant figures.
1. (2 points) How many molecules are in 0.725 mol of SO₂?
2. (2 points) Find the molar mass of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂.
3. (3 points) Find the mass of 0.450 mol of K₂CO₃.
4. (3 points) How many moles are in 30.0 g of KCl?
5. (4 points) Balance each equation.
(a) ___ C₂H₄ + ___ O₂ → ___ CO₂ + ___ H₂O
(b) ___ Al + ___ HCl → ___ AlCl₃ + ___ H₂
6. (4 points) 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O
(a) How many moles of H₂O form from 1.40 mol NH₃?
(b) How many moles of O₂ react with 1.40 mol NH₃?
7. (5 points) 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. What mass of CO₂ forms when 20.0 g of NaHCO₃ is heated?
8. (8 points) 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. A mixture has 5.00 g Fe and 6.00 g Cl₂.
(a) Find the moles of FeCl₃ that the Fe could make.
(b) Find the moles of FeCl₃ that the Cl₂ could make.
(c) Name the limiting reactant.
(d) Find the theoretical yield of FeCl₃ in grams.
9. (4 points) A student collects 7.80 g of FeCl₃ from the reaction in question 8.
(a) Find the percent yield.
(b) Give one reason the student collected less than the theoretical yield.
10. (5 points) 2C + O₂ → 2CO. A mixture has 3.00 g C and 3.20 g O₂. A student says C is limiting because 3.00 g is less than 3.20 g. Is the student correct? Show the calculation.

ANSWER KEY
1. 0.725 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 4.37 × 10²³ molecules. 1 setup, 1 answer.
2. 40.08 + 2(14.01) + 6(16.00) = 164.10 g/mol. 1 atom counts, 1 answer.
3. Molar mass 2(39.10) + 12.01 + 3(16.00) = 138.21 g/mol; 0.450 mol × 138.21 g/mol = 62.2 g. 1 molar mass, 1 setup, 1 answer with unit.
4. Molar mass 39.10 + 35.45 = 74.55 g/mol; 30.0 g ÷ 74.55 g/mol = 0.402 mol. 1 molar mass, 1 setup, 1 answer with unit.
5. (a) 1, 3, 2, 2. (b) 2, 6, 2, 3. 2 points each; all coefficients must be correct. Accept a blank for 1.
6. (a) 1.40 × 6/4 = 2.10 mol H₂O. (b) 1.40 × 5/4 = 1.75 mol O₂. 2 points each: 1 ratio, 1 answer.
7. NaHCO₃ is 84.01 g/mol; 20.0 ÷ 84.01 = 0.238 mol; × 1/2 = 0.119 mol CO₂; × 44.01 g/mol = 5.24 g. 1 molar mass, 1 moles, 1 ratio, 1 mass setup, 1 answer with unit. A student who uses the 1 : 1 ratio from the vinegar lab gets 10.5 g and loses only the ratio point.
8. (a) 5.00 ÷ 55.85 = 0.0895 mol Fe; × 2/2 = 0.0895 mol FeCl₃. (2: 1 moles, 1 ratio) (b) Cl₂ is 70.90 g/mol; 6.00 ÷ 70.90 = 0.0846 mol; × 2/3 = 0.0564 mol FeCl₃. (2: 1 moles, 1 ratio) (c) Cl₂, because it makes less FeCl₃. (1) (d) FeCl₃ is 55.85 + 3(35.45) = 162.20 g/mol; 0.0564 mol × 162.20 g/mol = 9.15 g. (3: 1 uses the limiting reactant, 1 molar mass, 1 answer with unit)
9. (a) 7.80 ÷ 9.15 × 100% = 85.2%. (3: 1 formula with actual over theoretical, 1 numbers, 1 answer) Mark from the student’s own answer to 8(d). (b) Any one of an incomplete reaction, product left on glassware or filter paper, or a side reaction. (1)
10. C: 3.00 ÷ 12.01 = 0.250 mol; × 2/2 = 0.250 mol CO. O₂: 3.20 ÷ 32.00 = 0.100 mol; × 2/1 = 0.200 mol CO. O₂ makes less CO, so O₂ limits and the student is not correct. 1 for each mole conversion, 1 for each ratio, 1 for the conclusion.

Collect every paper. Leave nothing worked on the board.

Students who finish early check their work quietly before handing in their tests. After all tests have been collected, distribute the reflection half sheets.
On a half sheet, students write one type of problem they felt sure about and one they want to revisit. They put their name on the sheet.
Collect the half sheets and keep them with the tests.
Tell students the marked tests come back with points for each question, and that no homework is set today.
segments.teacherNotes: Half sheets are ungraded and help plan any review. Do not discuss test answers aloud while other students may still be finishing. Check every paper has a name before students leave.

keyIdeas: Mass-to-mass stoichiometry problems follow one chain: grams to moles using molar mass, moles to moles using the coefficients, moles back to grams.

Setups with units and answers to three significant figures show clear chemical thinking and earn the points.

study.overview: You have sat the unit test, so this guide gives you a short reference for the skills it covered. Every stoichiometry problem comes down to the same few moves: use molar mass to switch between grams and moles, and use the coefficients of a balanced equation to switch between substances. Read each point, then try the same steps on your own problems. Your marked test will come back with points for each question.

points.heading: Follow the chain from grams to moles to moles to grams
points.explanation: Mass-to-mass problems follow one chain: grams to moles using molar mass, moles to moles using the coefficients, then moles back to grams. Write the units in every step so you can see them cancel. Example, with a different reaction: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Suppose you want the mass of water from 4.00 g of H₂. Molar mass of H₂ is 2.02 g/mol, so 4.00 g ÷ 2.02 g/mol = 1.98 mol H₂. The coefficients are 2 H₂ to 2 H₂O, so the ratio is 2/2 and you get 1.98 mol H₂O. Molar mass of H₂O is 2(1.01) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol, so 1.98 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 35.7 g H₂O. Using the class table of rounded atomic masses and giving the answer to three significant figures keeps your work consistent. Also remember that the mole links to particles: 1 mol is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, so 0.500 mol of CO₂ holds 0.500 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.

points.heading: Find the limiting reactant by comparing moles of the same product
points.explanation: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first. To find it, work out how many moles of the same product each reactant could make, then pick the reactant that makes less. Do not compare the starting grams, because that can mislead. Example, with a different reaction: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, starting with 2.40 g Mg and 2.40 g O₂. The grams are equal, so grams tell you nothing. Mg: 2.40 ÷ 24.31 = 0.0987 mol Mg, and the ratio 2/2 gives 0.0987 mol MgO. O₂: 2.40 ÷ 32.00 = 0.0750 mol O₂, and the ratio 2/1 gives 0.150 mol MgO. Mg makes less MgO, so Mg is the limiting reactant. The other reactant, O₂, is in excess.

points.heading: Get theoretical yield from the limiting reactant, then find percent yield
points.explanation: The theoretical yield is the most product the reaction could make, and it comes from the limiting reactant, never from the one in excess. In the magnesium example, the limiting reactant gives 0.0987 mol MgO. Molar mass of MgO is 24.31 + 16.00 = 40.31 g/mol, so the theoretical yield is 0.0987 × 40.31 = 3.98 g. Percent yield compares what you really got with that maximum: percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%. Suppose a student collects 3.40 g of MgO. Then 3.40 ÷ 3.98 × 100% = 85.4%. A real result is usually lower than the theoretical yield. Common reasons are an incomplete reaction, product left on glassware or filter paper, or a side reaction.

points.heading: Show clear setups, and balance with the smallest whole numbers
points.explanation: Points go to clear chemical thinking, so write the formula or setup, then the numbers with units, then the answer to three significant figures. If an earlier value is wrong but you carry it through correctly, your method can still earn credit, and a missing unit on a final answer can cost a point. Before any mole-ratio step, check that the equation is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients. Count atoms on each side. Example: N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ has 2 N on the left and 1 on the right, so put 2 in front of NH₃. Now there are 6 H on the right, so put 3 in front of H₂. The result is N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, and the mole ratios are 1 : 3 : 2. Use your reflection half sheet as a guide: choose the type of problem you want to revisit and practice a few more of that kind.

t_e499d3b3793b.prompt: A classmate says: ‘A mole of lead atoms must contain more particles than a mole of helium atoms, because lead atoms are so much heavier.’ Do you agree or disagree? Decide where you stand, then defend your position using what a mole is.
followUps: What exactly is a mole a measure of: a number, a mass, or a size? How do you know?
If 1 mol of lead atoms and 1 mol of helium atoms hold the same number of particles, what could still make the two samples different?
How is this like comparing a dozen eggs with a dozen bowling balls?

t_a46cbd21fd91.prompt: A student solves this problem: ‘How many moles are in 3.01 × 10²³ atoms of Al?’ and gets 1.81 × 10⁴⁷ mol by multiplying. Another student divides and gets 0.500 mol. Which answer would you trust, and what could you check to prove it without redoing the whole calculation?
followUps: Look at the unit setup. Which units cancel when you multiply, and which cancel when you divide?
Is a number of moles usually small or huge? Is a number of particles usually small or huge? Does 1.81 × 10⁴⁷ pass that check?
What rule would you give a friend so they always know whether to multiply or divide by 6.022 × 10²³?

t_3c9ab508fe08.prompt: What does one mole of particles represent?
t_3c9ab508fe08.explanation: A mole is an amount equal to 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

t_4f9ff9bdc712.prompt: A mole can count atoms, molecules, or formula units.
t_4f9ff9bdc712.explanation: The word mole names an amount, and the particles can be atoms, molecules, or formula units.

t_8fca5cdbf7b5.prompt: How many argon atoms are in 0.600 mol of argon atoms?
t_8fca5cdbf7b5.explanation: Multiply the amount in moles by 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole: 0.600 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.61 × 10²³ atoms.

t_eba12be2da54.prompt: To convert a number of particles to moles, multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole.
t_eba12be2da54.explanation: Divide the number of particles by 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole to find moles.

t_1c6359e92a28.prompt: How many total atoms are in 0.350 mol of NH₃ molecules?
t_1c6359e92a28.explanation: Each NH₃ molecule contains four atoms. Multiply 0.350 mol by 6.022 × 10²³ molecules per mole, then by 4 atoms per molecule.

t_4c465911370e.prompt: One mole of sodium atoms weighs 22.99 g and one mole of water molecules weighs 18.02 g. Both hold 6.022 × 10²³ particles. A classmate says, ‘If the numbers of particles are the same, the masses should be the same too.’ Do you agree? Decide with your partner, then defend your position to another pair.
followUps: What differs between a sodium atom and a water molecule that could change the mass of a mole of each?
Which is heavier, one sodium atom or one water molecule? How do the molar masses help you decide?
Is a mole a number or a mass? How does your answer change what ‘molar mass’ means?

t_744af7f14e27.prompt: A student finds the molar mass of Ca(OH)₂ and writes 40.08 + 16.00 + 1.01 = 57.09 g/mol. Another student writes 74.10 g/mol. Which answer is right, and how do you know? What would you tell the first student to check, and why does it matter when we later turn grams into moles?
followUps: How many atoms of each element are in one formula unit of Ca(OH)₂? What does the 2 outside the parentheses apply to?
How could a table with columns for element, atoms in the formula, molar mass and subtotal help catch this kind of error?
If a sample is weighed in grams, how would a wrong molar mass change the number of particles we calculate?

t_d60d387fff3f.prompt: The periodic table lists iron with an atomic mass of 55.85. What is the molar mass of iron?
t_d60d387fff3f.explanation: For an element, its atomic mass gives the molar mass in g/mol.

t_ffbffec7adfb.prompt: How many nitrogen and oxygen atoms are in Fe(NO₃)₃?
t_ffbffec7adfb.explanation: The subscript 3 outside the parentheses multiplies both the one nitrogen atom and the three oxygen atoms inside.

t_c0b927d3da82.prompt: Which statement describes what molar mass links together?

choices.text: Mass in grams and number of atoms only
Number of moles and reaction speed
Atomic mass units and number of moles
Mass in grams and number of particles

t_c0b927d3da82.explanation: Molar mass connects a sample’s mass in grams to its number of particles through the mole.

t_80bf3462403e.prompt: Find the molar mass of potassium sulfide, K₂S. Use K = 39.10 g/mol and S = 32.06 g/mol.
t_80bf3462403e.explanation: The formula contains two potassium atoms and one sulfur atom, so add their contributions.

t_aac98e21f8b8.prompt: In one sentence, explain why one mole of iron atoms and one mole of oxygen atoms have the same number of particles but different masses.
t_aac98e21f8b8.answer: Each mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, but iron atoms and oxygen atoms have different masses.
t_aac98e21f8b8.explanation: A mole fixes the number of particles, while the type of particle determines the mass of that mole.

t_29e3c146316a.prompt: A classmate says: “I have 10.0 g of aluminum foil, so I can just multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ to get the number of atoms. Why bother with moles?” Do you agree? Argue for or against, and use the foil example to support your side.
followUps: What unit would your answer have if you multiplied 10.0 g by 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol? Does that unit make sense?
Where does 26.98 g/mol enter the setup, and what job does it do in the chain?
How would you explain to your classmate why mass never converts directly to particles?

t_cd82e37456e8.prompt: Two students find the mass of 2.00 mol of H₂O. One writes 2.00 ÷ 18.02 and the other writes 2.00 × 18.02. Which setup is correct, and how can you tell without a calculator? Debate whether checking the unit cancellation or checking the size of the answer is the better way to catch a mistake.
followUps: In your setup, which unit goes on the bottom of the molar mass factor, and why?
Would the answer to 2.00 mol of water be bigger or smaller than 2.00 grams? Does that help you decide?
Can you think of a mistake that a size check would miss but unit cancellation would catch, or the other way around?

t_9ee3d6a62656.title: Problem set 1: Moles, mass, and particles
t_9ee3d6a62656.prompt: Show your work for each problem. Use the rounded atomic masses on your periodic table, include units in every step, and give molar masses to two decimal places and other final answers to three significant figures. This problem set is due at the start of next class.
steps: Find the molar mass of calcium chloride, CaCl₂. Show the contribution from each element and include the unit.
Convert 18.0 g of ammonia, NH₃, to moles. Show a dimensional-analysis setup with units that cancel.
Convert 0.425 mol of potassium bromide, KBr, to grams. Show a dimensional-analysis setup with units that cancel.
Find the number of sulfur atoms in a 12.0 g sample. Show both steps: convert grams to moles, then moles to atoms using 6.022 × 10²³ atoms per mole. Check whether the size of your answer makes sense.

t_888828e6eadb.prompt: Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, has a molar mass of 100.09 g/mol. How many moles are in 18.0 g of CaCO₃?
t_888828e6eadb.explanation: Divide the mass by the molar mass: 18.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.180 mol to three significant figures.

t_9b7138f3a658.prompt: Nitrogen gas, N₂, has a molar mass of 28.02 g/mol. What is the mass of 0.400 mol N₂?
t_9b7138f3a658.explanation: Multiply moles by molar mass: 0.400 mol × 28.02 g/mol = 11.2 g to three significant figures.

t_516e66cab48f.prompt: Which setup converts 6.00 g of calcium into calcium atoms? Calcium has a molar mass of 40.08 g/mol.
t_516e66cab48f.explanation: The molar mass factor cancels grams and leaves moles. The Avogadro factor then cancels moles and leaves atoms.

t_a836bc7f85e1.prompt: Neon has a molar mass of 20.18 g/mol. How many neon atoms are in a 7.50 g sample? Give your answer to three significant figures.
t_a836bc7f85e1.explanation: Convert grams to moles, then convert moles to atoms using 6.022 × 10²³ atoms per mole.

t_66064acff0c2.prompt: A student has 5.00 g of iodine and needs the number of iodine atoms. Name the two conversion steps and the unit that cancels in each step.
t_66064acff0c2.answer: Convert grams to moles using molar mass so grams cancel. Then convert moles to atoms using 6.022 × 10²³ atoms per mole so moles cancel.
t_66064acff0c2.explanation: Mass converts to particles through moles: first use molar mass, then use Avogadro’s number.

t_78d0d9375629.prompt: A classmate balances H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂O₂ on the right. Both sides now show 2 H and 2 O, so the atom counts match. Is this a fair way to balance the equation? Argue for or against, using what a subscript and a coefficient each tell us.
followUps: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance from water. If the atom counts match, why is the equation still not describing the reaction we started with?
What does the 2 in 2H₂O multiply? How many H atoms and how many O atoms does it give?
If a student insists that changing a subscript is just a shortcut, what question could you ask to make them see that the substance has changed?

t_561f6db9e7e0.prompt: Two students balance Al + CuCl₂ → AlCl₃ + Cu. One starts by balancing chlorine, the other starts with aluminum. Both reach 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu. Does the order matter? Which element would you balance first, which would you leave for last, and why?
followUps: Chlorine is 2 on the left and 3 on the right. How does a common multiple of 2 and 3 help, and why does it give 6 Cl on each side?
Why is it easier to leave an element that appears alone, such as Cu, until last?
If you get a fraction as a coefficient partway through, what can you do to keep whole numbers, and why must you recount afterward?

t_558b62560cf9.prompt: Which change is allowed when balancing a chemical equation?

choices.text: Change a subscript in a formula
Add a coefficient before a formula
Remove an element from a formula

t_558b62560cf9.explanation: Coefficients change how many units of a substance are present. Changing a subscript changes the substance.

t_701753d097c1.prompt: Which equation correctly balances K + H₂O → KOH + H₂?
t_701753d097c1.explanation: Both sides have 2 K, 4 H, and 2 O atoms.

t_23e0c3330782.prompt: Which equation correctly balances Na₂CO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂?
t_23e0c3330782.explanation: This equation has 2 Na, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H, and 2 Cl atoms on each side.

t_673c1047f7bd.prompt: Changing a subscript is an acceptable way to balance an equation because it keeps the element symbols the same.
t_673c1047f7bd.explanation: Changing a subscript changes the substance. Balance an equation by changing coefficients.

t_56584f352d9d.prompt: Explain how matching the number of each kind of atom on both sides of a balanced equation shows conservation of mass.
t_56584f352d9d.answer: The same atoms are present on both sides, so they have the same total mass; the atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
t_56584f352d9d.explanation: A reaction rearranges atoms. When each kind of atom is counted equally on both sides, the total mass is conserved.

t_7e53ffe4a9a1.prompt: A classmate says: “In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the coefficients are 2 and 1, so 2 g of H₂ react with 1 g of O₂.” Is this true? Decide in your pair, then defend your answer using the masses you found last time. Be ready to say exactly what the coefficients count.
followUps: Which numbers did you use to test the claim, and what did they show? (Look for 2 mol H₂ is 4.04 g and 1 mol O₂ is 32.00 g.)
If the claim is wrong, what would a student have to do first to use the coefficients correctly with a mass?
Why might the claim feel believable, even though it is not true?

t_0aa37d2587dc.prompt: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, a student must find the moles of H₂ needed for 1.50 mol N₂. One student writes 1.50 mol N₂ × (3 mol H₂ / 1 mol N₂). Another writes 1.50 mol N₂ × (1 mol N₂ / 3 mol H₂). Argue for which setup is right, and explain how you could convince someone who picked the other one without just giving the answer.
followUps: Which unit cancels in each setup, and which unit is left over?
Before you calculate, should the answer be bigger or smaller than 1.50 mol? How do the coefficients tell you?
What does it tell you if a mole ratio is inverted, and how would you spot it in a classmate’s work?

t_0a2cb14c9c77.title: Problem set 2: Mole ratios and reaction amounts
t_0a2cb14c9c77.prompt: Show your work for each problem. Use the rounded atomic masses on your periodic table, include units in every step, and give final answers to three significant figures. This problem set is due at the start of next class.
steps: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, write the mole ratio of AlCl₃ to Cl₂ as a fraction.
For CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, calculate how many moles of CO₂ form from 0.625 mol CaCO₃. Show the mole ratio and a unit setup.
For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, calculate how many moles of MgO form from 1.20 mol O₂. Show the mole ratio and a unit setup.
For 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃, calculate how many moles of O₂ react with 13.5 g Al. Convert grams of Al to moles first, then use the mole ratio. Show units in each step.

t_380caa3a818c.prompt: For 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, which mole ratio gives mol SO₃ per mol SO₂?
t_380caa3a818c.explanation: Use the coefficients of SO₃ and SO₂, in that order.

t_8dbda23d1075.prompt: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, which factor converts mol Al to mol Cl₂?
t_8dbda23d1075.explanation: Put the wanted unit, mol Cl₂, on top so mol Al cancels.

t_1a7843c2977e.prompt: For 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, how many moles of SO₃ form from 0.350 mol O₂?
t_1a7843c2977e.explanation: Multiply by the ratio 2 mol SO₃ per 1 mol O₂.

t_a69c9b2500ba.prompt: A student claims that 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ in a balanced equation mean 2 g H₂ react with 1 g O₂. What do the coefficients count, and what must you do before using an equation to compare masses?
t_a69c9b2500ba.answer: The coefficients give mole ratios. Convert each mass to moles before using the balanced equation.
t_a69c9b2500ba.explanation: Balanced equation coefficients count moles of particles, not grams.

t_1981708ba51e.prompt: For Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, how many moles of H₂ form from 0.800 mol HCl?
t_1981708ba51e.explanation: The mole ratio is 1 mol H₂ per 2 mol HCl.

t_573568738ed1.prompt: A classmate says: “If mass is conserved, the cup of fizzing vinegar should weigh the same before and after. So the balance reading must be wrong, or the law doesn’t apply to open cups.” Do you agree? Decide where you stand, then explain what the balance reading does and does not tell you.

Another student says, “The mass lost equals the mass of baking soda that reacted.” What evidence from the equation and the molar masses shows that these are different quantities?

t_71a16fa4848a.prompt: Your measured CO₂ is 0.08 g lower than your predicted CO₂. One partner says the mole-ratio prediction must be wrong. The other says the procedure caused the gap. Which explanation would you defend, and what would you need to see in your data or at the bench to be convinced?
followUps: List every explanation you can find in the procedure. For each one, would it make the measured CO₂ lower or higher than the prediction? Which does your evidence support best?
What if your measured value were a little higher than predicted? Which explanations still work, and which no longer do?
How would leaving the boat off the final weighing change the measured mass of CO₂, and in which direction?

t_dea85bc1518c.prompt: A cup of vinegar and a weigh boat holding baking soda are weighed together before mixing. After the reaction, the same cup and boat are weighed with the remaining liquid. The final mass is lower. What does the mass lost estimate?

choices.text: The mass of baking soda that reacted
The mass of vinegar that evaporated
The mass of carbon dioxide released
The mass of sodium acetate formed

t_dea85bc1518c.explanation: Carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air. With the same cup, boat, and remaining liquid included in both readings, the decrease estimates the gas released.

t_a121ee67cf76.prompt: Which set of readings lets a pair find the mass of baking soda used and the mass lost during the reaction?

choices.text: Empty boat, boat with soda, starting total, final total without the boat
Empty boat, boat with soda, starting total, final total with the boat
Boat with soda, starting total, final total with the boat, vinegar volume
Empty boat, starting total, final total with the boat, vinegar volume

t_a121ee67cf76.explanation: Subtract the empty boat mass from the boat-with-soda mass to find the soda mass. Subtract the final total from the starting total to estimate the carbon dioxide mass; the boat must be included both times.

t_0d89c6aca712.prompt: A pair uses 1.68 g of NaHCO₃. Using 84.01 g/mol for NaHCO₃ and 44.01 g/mol for CO₂, predict the mass of CO₂. Use the 1:1 mole ratio and round the final answer to three significant figures.
t_0d89c6aca712.explanation: Convert the NaHCO₃ mass to moles, use the 1:1 ratio to get moles of CO₂, then convert those moles to grams.

t_e5dcc926b4c3.prompt: A pair predicts 0.92 g of CO₂ and measures 0.84 g from the mass lost. What is the difference between the predicted and measured masses?
t_e5dcc926b4c3.explanation: Find the difference by subtracting the measured mass from the predicted mass: 0.92 g − 0.84 g = 0.08 g.

t_189023e8f495.prompt: A pair forgets to put the weigh boat back on the balance for the final weighing. Will their measured mass of CO₂ come out too high or too low? Explain.
t_189023e8f495.answer: Too high. The boat’s mass is missing from the final reading, so it is counted as part of the mass lost.
t_189023e8f495.explanation: Measured CO₂ is the starting mass minus the final mass. Leaving the boat off makes the final mass smaller, so the difference comes out larger than the mass of CO₂ that escaped.

t_4901acf62244.prompt: A shop has 10 wheels and 8 frames, and each bike needs 2 wheels and 1 frame. A classmate says, “Frames are fewer than wheels, so frames run out first.” Do you agree? Decide which runs out first, then say whether the same reasoning would work for 4.00 g H₂ and 16.00 g O₂ in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Defend your answer with numbers.
followUps: What did you compare in the bike shop, and what is the matching quantity in the chemistry problem?
Is the reactant with less mass ever the limiting one? What would you need to check before you say it is?
How would you convince a classmate who says that comparing grams is quicker?

t_4d2c293c7ce7.prompt: Two students solve the same problem: how many grams of NH₃ form from 14.0 g N₂ when H₂ is in excess, using N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Student A uses the coefficient 3 when changing grams of N₂ to moles. Student B divides 14.0 g by 28.02 g/mol first, and only then uses the coefficients. Which steps in the chain use coefficients, and which use the periodic table? Whose setup do you trust, and why?
followUps: Where does the unit cancellation show that Student A’s setup goes wrong?
Which coefficients matter in the mole ratio: only those of the two substances in the question, or all of them? Explain.
If a problem says nothing about an excess reactant, what would you need to check first before using the three-step chain?

t_137302211882.prompt: Which sequence shows the three steps in a mass-to-mass conversion?

choices.text: grams of reactant → moles of reactant → moles of product → grams of product
grams of reactant → moles of reactant → grams of product → moles of product
grams of reactant → grams of reactant → moles of product → grams of product
grams of reactant → moles of product → moles of reactant → grams of product

t_137302211882.explanation: Convert grams to moles using molar mass, use the coefficients for the mole ratio, then convert product moles to grams using molar mass.

t_b29b8e185f97.prompt: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, 5.40 g Al reacts with 18.0 g Cl₂. Which reactant is limiting, based on the amount of AlCl₃ each could produce?

choices.text: Al; it could make 0.200 mol AlCl₃
Cl₂; it could make 0.169 mol AlCl₃
Al; it could make 0.169 mol AlCl₃
Cl₂; it could make 0.200 mol AlCl₃

t_b29b8e185f97.explanation: The Al could make about 0.200 mol AlCl₃. The Cl₂ could make about 0.169 mol. The smaller possible product amount identifies Cl₂ as limiting.

t_e94e8dc7230e.prompt: Only the mole-ratio step in a mass-to-mass chain uses equation coefficients.
t_e94e8dc7230e.explanation: The two other steps use molar masses to convert between grams and moles.

t_1d34c1ca06e9.prompt: After finding which reactant is in excess, how do you find how much of it remains?

choices.text: Subtract the starting amount from the amount that reacted
Add the amount that reacted to the amount you started with
Subtract the amount that reacted from the amount you started with
Divide the amount that reacted by the amount you started with

t_1d34c1ca06e9.explanation: Use the mole ratio to find how much excess reactant reacted, then subtract that from its starting amount.

t_ff18a67d4285.prompt: Potassium chlorate decomposes according to 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Using K = 39.10, Cl = 35.45, and O = 16.00, how many grams of O₂ form from 12.3 g KClO₃? Give your answer to three significant figures.
t_ff18a67d4285.explanation: Convert KClO₃ to moles, use the 3:2 mole ratio to find moles of O₂, then convert O₂ to grams.

t_603cb5be316b.title: Problem set 3: Mass-to-mass and limiting reactants
t_603cb5be316b.prompt: Show your work for each problem. Use the rounded atomic masses on your periodic table, include units in every step, and give final answers to three significant figures. This problem set is due at the start of next class.
steps: For 2K + Br₂ → 2KBr, calculate the mass of KBr formed from 6.50 g K when Br₂ is in excess. Show the three-step conversion.
For 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, use 5.40 g Al and 8.00 g Fe₂O₃. Calculate the moles of Fe each reactant could produce, then identify the limiting reactant.
Using the same reaction and starting masses, calculate the moles of Fe produced and the moles of Al left over.
For C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O, use 10.0 g C₃H₈ and 32.0 g O₂. Identify the limiting reactant, then calculate the moles of C₃H₈ left over and the mass of CO₂ produced.

t_dda7be2edbcd.prompt: A student collects 0.400 g of copper when the theoretical yield is 0.473 g, so the percent yield is 84.6%. One student says, ‘That is a bad result, because a careful chemist would get 100%.’ Another says, ‘A percent yield of about 85% is actually good, and 100% would make me suspicious.’ Which student do you agree with, and why? What would you need to know to judge whether the result is acceptable?
followUps: Which would worry you more: a result of 84.6% or a result of 112%? What does each one tell you about the experiment?
If the student had left some copper stuck on the filter paper, would that change the actual yield, the theoretical yield, or both? Explain.
Is it possible for a perfectly careful student to get exactly 100%? What would have to be true?

t_6dbb4f55651c.prompt: Two students each get a percent yield of 85% in the baking soda and vinegar lab. One says the reaction did not finish. The other says some CO₂ dissolved in the vinegar and was never measured. Both explanations seem sensible. Can the class tell which is right from the percent yield alone? What evidence or change to the procedure would help decide between them?
followUps: Is a gas that dissolves in the liquid an example of an incomplete reaction, of loss in handling, or of something else? Defend your choice.
How could you test whether the reaction had finished, for example by adding more vinegar and watching for more bubbles?
Could both explanations be true at once? How would that affect the percent yield?

t_07c090890bde.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes actual yield from theoretical yield?

choices.text: Actual yield is collected and measured; theoretical yield is calculated from the limiting reactant.
Actual yield is calculated from the limiting reactant; theoretical yield is collected and measured.
Actual yield is the reactant mass used; theoretical yield is the product mass collected.
Actual yield is the product mass possible; theoretical yield is the product mass collected.

t_07c090890bde.explanation: Actual yield is the product mass really collected. Theoretical yield is the product mass calculated from the limiting reactant.

t_82050c1e747d.prompt: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.40 g and an actual yield of 6.72 g. Calculate the percent yield. Give your answer to three significant figures.
t_82050c1e747d.explanation: Divide actual yield by theoretical yield, then multiply by 100%.

t_236c1644b24f.prompt: A solid product remains on the filter paper after collection. Which source of low yield does this describe?
t_236c1644b24f.explanation: Product left on filter paper was not collected, so the actual yield is lower.

t_bfe62f40907c.prompt: Explain how an incomplete reaction and product lost during handling can each lower percent yield.
t_bfe62f40907c.answer: An incomplete reaction leaves some reactant unconverted, so less product forms. Product lost during handling, such as product left on glassware, is not collected, so the measured actual yield is lower.
t_bfe62f40907c.explanation: Both causes reduce the actual yield compared with the theoretical yield, but one reduces product formed and the other reduces product collected.

t_f85a23cb308a.prompt: A student calculates a percent yield above 100%. Which explanation best fits this result?

choices.text: The reaction may have stopped before completion.
Some product may have stayed on glassware.
The actual yield may be below the theoretical yield.
The collected product may be wet or impure.

t_f85a23cb308a.explanation: Wet or impure material can make the measured product mass too high, producing a value above 100%.

t_804867f498aa.title: Problem set 4: Percent yield and product loss
t_804867f498aa.prompt: Show your work for each problem. Use the rounded atomic masses on your periodic table, include units in every step, and give final answers to three significant figures. This problem set is due at the start of next class.
steps: For CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, 5.60 g CaO reacts with excess water. Calculate the theoretical mass of Ca(OH)₂, then find the percent yield if 6.40 g Ca(OH)₂ is collected. Show the conversion chain.
For 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂, 6.20 g Mg is heated with 3.40 g N₂. Find the limiting reactant and the theoretical mass of Mg₃N₂, then find the percent yield if 7.55 g Mg₃N₂ is collected.

A student filters, dries and weighs a solid product. The theoretical yield is 9.00 g and the weighed mass is 9.36 g. Calculate the percent yield and explain why this result points to an error. Give one likely cause.
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.00 g and an actual yield of 7.20 g. Calculate the percent yield and explain two ways the actual yield could be lower than the theoretical yield.

t_453af44b61aa.prompt: Imagine a student says, “Showing my setup with units costs me time, and I can do the arithmetic in my head, so only my final answer should count.” Do you agree? Decide where you stand, then defend it to a classmate who disagrees. Think about what a setup shows that a final answer alone cannot.
followUps: Suppose two students both get a wrong final answer, but one wrote a clear setup with units and the other wrote only a number. Which paper tells you more about what the student understands, and why?
Where in a mass-to-mass problem could a missing unit hide a mistake, such as mixing up grams and moles?
How does a clear setup help you find your own error when you check your work at the end?

t_9bedf341047d.prompt: A student claims, “The reactant with the smaller mass is always the limiting reactant, because there is less of it.” Argue for or against this claim. What would you need to know about the reactants before you could decide which one runs out first?
followUps: Suppose one reactant has a small mass but a very large molar mass, and the other has a larger mass but a small molar mass. Which comparison would you make, and why does it work better than comparing grams?
Why must you compare the moles of the same product that each reactant could make, rather than just comparing their moles?
If the claim turned out to be wrong for some reaction, what does that tell you about how you should check any limiting reactant problem in the future?

t_119a9867ddcf.prompt: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, aluminum is in excess. How many moles of AlCl₃ can form from 0.900 mol Cl₂?
t_119a9867ddcf.explanation: The coefficient ratio is 2 mol AlCl₃ for every 3 mol Cl₂, so 0.900 × 2/3 = 0.600 mol AlCl₃.

t_addc15758cad.prompt: Using the class atomic masses, find the mass of 0.275 mol MgCl₂. Give your answer to three significant figures.
t_addc15758cad.explanation: MgCl₂ has a molar mass of 24.31 + 2(35.45) = 95.21 g/mol. Multiply by the given amount in moles.

t_cf15cd260fc7.prompt: For 2Fe + 3S → Fe₂S₃, a mixture contains 2.00 mol Fe and 2.00 mol S. Which reactant is limiting?
t_cf15cd260fc7.explanation: Iron could make 1.00 mol Fe₂S₃. Sulfur could make 0.667 mol Fe₂S₃. Sulfur makes less product, so it is limiting.

t_801e20ba9d6c.prompt: Theoretical yield is calculated from the reactant that can make the greatest amount of product.
t_801e20ba9d6c.explanation: The limiting reactant makes the smaller amount of product, and theoretical yield is calculated from that reactant.

t_1f20cceabf26.prompt: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 12.0 g and an actual yield of 9.60 g. Which setup finds the percent yield?
t_1f20cceabf26.explanation: Percent yield is actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100%.

t_7568d04d46dc.title: Lab report: carbon dioxide from baking soda and vinegar
t_7568d04d46dc.prompt: Write a 1–2 page lab report about your baking soda and vinegar experiment. Use your own recorded measurements to report the mass of carbon dioxide released and compare it with the predicted mass. Explain what your results show using evidence from your data and details of the procedure.
steps: State the purpose of the experiment and describe how you measured the mass change.
Include your recorded masses and show how you found the mass of baking soda used and the measured mass of carbon dioxide.
Show how you predicted the carbon dioxide mass from the sodium bicarbonate mass, molar masses, and the 1:1 mole ratio.
Compare the measured and predicted carbon dioxide masses by finding their difference in grams. Explain possible differences using your data and the procedure.

t_f42cc5ca3931.prompt: In our two setups, aluminum has the smaller mass both times, yet it limits in only one. A classmate says, “The reactant you have less of must run out first.” Is that claim true, false, or only sometimes true? Defend your answer using the coefficients in 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu and the molar masses of aluminum and copper(II) chloride dihydrate.
followUps: Aluminum is 26.98 g/mol and the salt is 170.5 g/mol. How does that gap change what a gram of each reactant means?
In the model with 0.80 g Al and 3.00 g CuCl₂·2H₂O, the aluminum has the smaller mass. What did the moles of copper each could make tell us?
What would you need to know about a new pair of reactants before you could trust a prediction based only on mass?

t_62770b9d909b.prompt: Your pair predicted a limiting reactant, but what you saw in the beaker seems to disagree with it. For example, foil is still there but the blue color is also still strong. Which should you trust more, your calculation or your observation? Argue for one side, then say what you would check before deciding.
followUps: Which reasons for a mismatch come from the calculation, and which come from the procedure, such as the oxide layer on the foil or a weighing slip?
If foil remains and the solution is blue or pale, what would you do next, and how long would you wait before deciding the reaction is finished?
Why do the foil and the color together make better evidence than either one alone?

t_272597b444f5.title: Lab report: limiting reactant with copper chloride and aluminum
t_272597b444f5.prompt: Write a 1–2 page lab report about the copper(II) chloride and aluminum experiment. Use your recorded measurements and observations to explain which reactant limited the reaction and how the evidence supports your conclusion. Add your dried copper mass after you weigh it next lesson.
steps: State the purpose of the experiment and describe how you prepared and reacted the copper(II) chloride solution and aluminum foil.
Include your recorded masses. Convert each reactant mass to moles and use 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu to show how much copper each reactant could produce.
Identify the predicted limiting reactant and the predicted mass of copper. Show the molar masses and mole ratios you used.
Describe your observations, including the solution color, whether foil remained, and the copper that formed. Use this evidence to confirm or question your prediction.
After you weigh your dried copper next lesson, compare it with the predicted mass. Explain possible differences using your measurements and details of the procedure.

t_14bc1643f3cb.prompt: A pair weighs 0.42 g of aluminum and 2.10 g of copper(II) chloride dihydrate. Which method predicts the limiting reactant?

choices.text: Compare the reactant masses and choose the smaller mass.
Compare the reactant coefficients and choose the smaller coefficient.
Convert both masses to moles and choose the larger mole amount.
Convert both masses to moles and compare the copper each could make.

t_14bc1643f3cb.explanation: The limiting reactant is the one that could make fewer moles of copper. Convert each mass to moles, then use the balanced equation coefficients.

t_f98453545ec2.prompt: A pair uses 0.36 g of aluminum and 1.20 g of copper(II) chloride dihydrate. Using 26.98 g/mol for aluminum, 170.5 g/mol for the dihydrate, and 63.55 g/mol for copper, calculate the predicted mass of copper. Round to 2 significant figures.
t_f98453545ec2.explanation: The dihydrate could make fewer moles of copper: 1.20 ÷ 170.5 = 0.00704 mol Cu. Aluminum could make about 0.0200 mol Cu, so the dihydrate limits. Its copper mass is about 0.45 g.

t_a49c504eefb0.prompt: The reactant with the smaller starting mass is always the limiting reactant.
t_a49c504eefb0.explanation: Mass alone does not identify the limiting reactant. Convert each reactant mass to moles and use the coefficients to compare how much copper each could make.

t_d79b5b0a5612.prompt: At the end of a reaction, the blue color has disappeared and a piece of foil remains. Which reactant was limiting?

choices.text: Copper(II) chloride was limiting because foil remained.
Aluminum was limiting because foil remained.
Aluminum was limiting because blue color disappeared.
Copper(II) chloride was limiting because copper formed.

t_d79b5b0a5612.explanation: When copper(II) chloride is limiting, its blue color fades and foil remains. Reddish-brown copper forms in either case.

t_44913a0018b3.prompt: At the end of a reaction, no foil remains and the solution is still blue. Name the limiting reactant and one observation that supports your answer. Also name the solid product you would expect to see.
t_44913a0018b3.answer: Aluminum is the limiting reactant. The foil is gone while the solution remains blue. Reddish-brown copper forms.
t_44913a0018b3.explanation: When aluminum is limiting, the foil disappears and the blue color remains. Reddish-brown copper forms either way.

f_602313ced031.question: Is a mole a mass or a number?
f_602313ced031.answer: A mole is a number, like a dozen. One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles. It does not name a mass or a kind of particle. The particles can be atoms, molecules or formula units.

f_9b92b6066514.question: How do I know whether to multiply or divide by 6.022 × 10²³?
f_9b92b6066514.answer: Write the conversion factor with units and cancel. If you start with moles, put mol in the denominator: 2.50 mol × (6.022 × 10²³ particles / 1 mol) = 1.51 × 10²⁴ molecules. If you start with particles, put particles in the denominator and divide. Then check: moles are usually small and particle counts are huge.

f_a4922ee3a2e1.question: Do 1 mol of water molecules and 1 mol of sodium atoms have the same number of particles?
f_a4922ee3a2e1.answer: Yes. Each sample holds 6.022 × 10²³ particles. A heavier atom does not make a mole contain more particles. Whether the two samples have the same mass is something we will return to later in the course.

f_1564c8c9b94d.question: Why does my calculator give a wrong answer with 6.022 × 10²³?
f_1564c8c9b94d.answer: Often the exponent was typed as ×10×23. Use the EE key (or EXP) to enter ×10²³, for example 6.022 EE 23. Then check that your answer has a sensible size.

f_859bf36d64d7.question: Why do I write g/mol after the number? Isn’t 12.01 enough?
f_859bf36d64d7.answer: No. The number alone is not a molar mass. Molar mass is a mass in grams for one mole, so the unit g/mol is part of the answer. Carbon is 12.01 g/mol. Without the unit, no one knows if you mean one atom, one mole or something else.

f_b45e2651f10d.question: When a formula has a subscript, like the 3 in NaHCO₃, what do I do with it?
f_b45e2651f10d.answer: The subscript tells you how many atoms of that element to count. In NaHCO₃ there are three O atoms, so you add 3 × 16.00 = 48.00 g/mol for oxygen. Then add Na 22.99, H 1.01 and C 12.01 to get 84.01 g/mol. A common mistake is counting O only once.

f_90fcc166d50b.question: How do I handle parentheses, like in Ca(OH)₂?
f_90fcc166d50b.answer: A subscript outside the parentheses multiplies every atom inside. Ca(OH)₂ has one Ca, two O and two H. Write it as 40.08 + 2 × (16.00 + 1.01) = 74.10 g/mol. Do not forget the 2 outside the parentheses.

f_466e55f87403.question: One mole of water and one mole of sodium both hold 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Why do they have different masses?
f_466e55f87403.answer: The number of particles is the same, but the particles are different. One mole of sodium atoms is 22.99 g and one mole of water molecules is 18.02 g. Molar mass links the mass you can weigh to the number of particles you cannot count.

f_cc1e657c489c.question: How do I know whether to multiply or divide by the molar mass?
f_cc1e657c489c.answer: Write the unit with every number and set up the factor so the unit you want to get rid of cancels. To turn 29.22 g NaCl into moles, put grams on the bottom: 29.22 g × (1 mol / 58.44 g) = 0.500 mol. To turn 2.00 mol H₂O into grams, put moles on the bottom: 2.00 mol × (18.02 g / 1 mol) = 36.0 g. The setup tells you the operation, so you do not have to guess.

f_df076c6646c4.question: Why can’t I go straight from grams to atoms or molecules?
f_df076c6646c4.answer: Mass does not convert directly to particles. The molar mass links grams to moles, and 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole links moles to particles. So use two steps: grams to moles, then moles to particles. For 10.0 g of aluminum, that is 10.0 ÷ 26.98 = 0.371 mol, and then 0.371 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.23 × 10²³ atoms.

f_254c502de2e8.question: How can I tell if my answer makes sense?
f_254c502de2e8.answer: Check its size. A few grams of a substance is usually a small fraction of a mole to a few moles, and the number of particles is very large, with an exponent around 10²² or 10²³. For 9.00 g of H₂O, a bit under half a mole (0.499 mol) is reasonable, since 9.00 g is about half of 18.02 g. If you get a huge number of moles or a small number of particles, check whether you skipped the mole step or flipped the molar mass factor.

f_f4f976ab3eb9.question: Why can’t I write H₂O₂ to fix the oxygen count in H₂ + O₂ → H₂O?
f_f4f976ab3eb9.answer: A subscript is part of the substance’s identity. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance from water. To balance an equation, change only the coefficients, the whole numbers in front of the formulas. For example, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 4 H and 2 O on each side.

f_ce3af1719095.question: What does a coefficient like the 2 in 2H₂O mean, and which element should I balance first?
f_ce3af1719095.answer: A coefficient multiplies the whole formula, so 2H₂O means 4 H and 2 O. Start with elements that appear in only one compound on each side. Leave an element that stands alone, such as O₂ in CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O or Cu in 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu, for last. Count the atoms, change one coefficient, then recount.

f_3be3b28ccdd3.question: How do I know when to stop, and what if I end up with a fraction?
f_3be3b28ccdd3.answer: Stop when every element has the same number of atoms on both sides, and use the smallest whole numbers that work. Recount once more to be sure. If a fraction appears, double every coefficient to clear it. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the mass also balances: 4.04 g of H₂ plus 32.00 g of O₂ equals 36.04 g of H₂O.

f_3dc531b7731d.question: Do I use the subscripts or the coefficients to write a mole ratio?
f_3dc531b7731d.answer: Use the coefficients. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the ratio of H₂ to O₂ is 2 mol H₂ / 1 mol O₂. The subscript 2 in H₂ tells you how many atoms are in one molecule, not how many moles react. If a substance has no written coefficient, the coefficient is 1.

f_7b5906e9eb66.question: How do I know which substance goes on top of the ratio?
f_7b5906e9eb66.answer: Put the substance you want on top and the substance you have on the bottom. Then the unit you have cancels. For 3.00 mol O₂ → mol H₂O, write 3.00 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂). The mol O₂ cancels and mol H₂O is left, giving 6.00 mol H₂O. If the unit you started with does not cancel, flip the ratio.

f_0b758366f52d.question: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, do 2 g of H₂ react with 1 g of O₂?
f_0b758366f52d.answer: No. The coefficients count moles, not grams. 2 mol H₂ is 4.04 g and 1 mol O₂ is 32.00 g. To use an equation with masses, convert the mass to moles first, then use the mole ratio.

f_8da3296dc11b.question: Why does the cup get lighter if mass is conserved?
f_8da3296dc11b.answer: Mass is conserved, but one product, carbon dioxide, is a gas and escapes into the air. It leaves the cup, so the mass on the balance goes down. The mass lost is the mass of CO₂ released.

f_68293bf60a66.question: Why must the same boat go back on the balance after the reaction?
f_68293bf60a66.answer: The final weighing must hold the same cup, the same liquid and the same boat as the starting weighing. If the boat is left off, its mass counts as lost, and your measured CO₂ will look too large. Only then does the mass difference mean CO₂ only.

f_b0142a6182e5.question: My measured CO₂ does not match my prediction. Did I do something wrong?
f_b0142a6182e5.answer: A gap does not mean you did something wrong. Measured and predicted values rarely match exactly. Find the difference in grams and note which value is larger. Then think back over the procedure: what could have kept CO₂ in the cup, and what besides CO₂ could have left it? Pick the reasons that fit what your pair did and that push the result in the direction you saw. Use your own measured values for the report.

f_37061f7e591f.question: Why do I use the molar mass of the substance I want, and not the one I started with, in the last step?
f_37061f7e591f.answer: The last step turns moles of the wanted substance into grams of it. So you multiply by the molar mass of that substance. In 14.0 g N₂ → NH₃, the first step divides by 28.02 g/mol (N₂) and the last step multiplies by 17.04 g/mol (NH₃). Only the middle step uses the coefficients.

f_42c3ac24020c.question: The reactant with less mass should run out first, so why was H₂ not the limiting reactant in the 4.00 g H₂ and 16.00 g O₂ problem?
f_42c3ac24020c.answer: Grams do not tell you which reactant runs out. Moles and coefficients do. Here 4.00 g H₂ is 1.98 mol and could make 1.98 mol of water. 16.00 g O₂ is 0.500 mol and could make only 1.00 mol of water. O₂ makes the smaller amount, so O₂ limits. H₂ has less mass but is in excess.

f_bec6d0be3565.question: How do I find how much of the excess reactant is left over?
f_bec6d0be3565.answer: First use the mole ratio to find how much of the excess reactant was used up by the limiting reactant. Then subtract that from the amount you started with. In the water example, 0.500 mol O₂ uses 1.00 mol H₂. You began with 1.98 mol H₂, so 0.980 mol (1.98 g) is left.

f_369df9270074.question: Why do we divide by the theoretical yield and not the actual yield?
f_369df9270074.answer: Percent yield asks what share of the possible product you got. The possible amount is the theoretical yield, so it goes on the bottom: actual ÷ theoretical × 100%. If you flip them, you get a number above 100% for a normal result, which is a sign you divided the wrong way.

f_6a689a3d0392.question: Which reactant do I use to find the theoretical yield?
f_6a689a3d0392.answer: Always start from the limiting reactant. It runs out first, so it sets the most product the reaction can make. Using the reactant that is in excess gives a theoretical yield that is too big, and your percent yield will come out too low.

f_b4bcd7ecae64.question: Can percent yield be more than 100%?
f_b4bcd7ecae64.answer: A correct result should not be. It would mean you collected more product than the limiting reactant could make. That usually points to an error, such as a product that was still wet or was mixed with other substances. Check your drying and your masses.

f_b477b93dabae.question: Do the actual and theoretical yields need to be in the same unit?
f_b477b93dabae.answer: Yes. Convert one of them first, for example both in grams. Then the units cancel and the percent yield has no unit other than the percent sign.

f_40011085fdfb.question: Can I use my own periodic table or formula sheet?
f_40011085fdfb.answer: No. Each desk has the class periodic table of rounded atomic masses and Avogadro’s number, 6.022 × 10²³. Use those values for molar masses. Your desk should be clear except for a pencil and a calculator. If you have no calculator, ask for a spare.

f_a1898150508b.question: How will my answers be marked, and do I lose points for a wrong answer?
f_a1898150508b.answer: The test is marked out of 40 points and is worth 50% of the course grade. Show every setup with units. You can earn method points even if an earlier value was wrong, as long as you carry it through correctly. Where an answer needs a unit, the point for that answer is withheld if the unit is missing. Give final calculated amounts and percent yields to three significant figures, and use the smallest whole-number coefficients when balancing.

f_cbdfeb6ddeff.question: What if I finish early or don’t understand a question?
f_cbdfeb6ddeff.answer: If you finish early, check your work quietly and then hand in your test. If a question’s wording is unclear, raise your hand. Your teacher can answer questions about wording only, not about how to solve a problem. After all tests are collected, you will write on a half sheet one type of problem you felt sure about and one you want to revisit. Put your name on it. The half sheet is not graded. No homework is set today.

f_99d30fc9b4df.question: Aluminum has the smaller mass in both setups. Why isn’t it the limiting reactant in both?
f_99d30fc9b4df.answer: Limiting reactants are found by comparing moles, not grams. Aluminum’s molar mass is small (26.98 g/mol), so even a small mass of foil is many moles. Change each mass to moles, use the coefficients to find the moles of Cu each reactant could make, and the smaller amount belongs to the limiting reactant. In one setup aluminum limits. In the other, copper(II) chloride does.

f_1fb32fcd623d.question: Why do we use 170.5 g/mol for the copper(II) chloride?
f_1fb32fcd623d.answer: The blue solid is the dihydrate, CuCl₂·2H₂O, which includes the water in its crystals. Its molar mass is 170.5 g/mol. One mole of the dihydrate gives 1 mole of CuCl₂ in solution, so the 3 to 3 ratio in the equation still applies.

f_90154c92c259.question: Why do we rinse the copper three times and wait to weigh it?
f_90154c92c259.answer: Each step protects the mass you will compare with your prediction. Think about what is on the copper before it is rinsed, and what is still in it before it is dry, and which way each would move the balance reading. The copper is left to dry until its mass stops changing. Next time you weigh the paper plus copper and subtract the paper’s mass. That is the copper mass for your lab report.
